contributions.text_english: There are questions to the Cabinet Minister for Health and Care tomorrow, so it would be appropriate for you to raise them tomorrow during that session. If there's no opportunity to do that, I would suggest that you write with all of your questions to the Minister directly.
contributions.text_original: Mae yna gwestiynau i'r Gweinidog Cabinet dros Iechyd a Gofal yfory, felly fe fyddai'n briodol i chi fod yn codi'r rhain yn ystod y sesiwn honno. Os na fydd yna gyfle, mi fuaswn i'n awgrymu eich bod chi'n ysgrifennu gyda'ch holl gwestiynau at y Gweinidog yn uniongyrchol.

contributions.text_english: Could I ask for a statement from the Government updating us on the work on the fire summit, please? I know that there was a very clear consensus in the Chamber when we had the statement from the First Minister that there should be involvement of those who worked at a grass-roots level—so, farmers and others who supported the firefighters in their efforts. I was concerned to see that, of the representatives from Blaenavon, just one has been included. Indeed, one of the key landowners has actually been uninvited. I'm also informed that the summit is only going to be for two hours. I would question whether that will be enough to deal with something as significant as this. So, could I ask the Trefnydd whether we could have an update on this?

contributions.text_english: Thank you for raising those issues. You will have heard the First Minister stating unambiguously the commitment of this Government to look at and learn the necessary lessons from those experiences. You will also know the order of business in this Senedd. With the concerns that you expresses, I would suggest that writing to the First Minister would be best, because they were very specific issues that you raised. I think, in looking at the business programme, perhaps there wouldn't be space for such a statement for a number of weeks, whereas the issues that you have raised suggest that you need an answer sooner than that. Clearly, we are committed to continuing to update this Senedd and we will do so with all Members on this crucial issue.
contributions.text_original: Diolch i chi am godi'r materion hynny. Mi fyddwch chi wedi clywed y Prif Weinidog yn gyfan gwbl ddiamwys o ran ymroddiad y Llywodraeth hon i fod yn edrych a dysgu'r gwersi angenrheidiol o hynny. Mi fyddwch chi'n gwybod hefyd trefn busnes y Senedd hon. Gyda'r pryderon rydych chi'n eu codi, mi fuaswn yn awgrymu mai ysgrifennu at y Prif Weinidog fyddai orau, gan fod yna bethau penodol iawn rydych chi wedi'u codi. Rwy'n credu, o edrych ar y rhaglen fusnes, ei bod hi'n bosibl na fydd lle am nifer o wythnosau am ddatganiad o'r fath, ac mae'r hyn rydych chi wedi'i godi yn awgrymu bod angen ateb arnoch yn gynt na hynny. Yn amlwg, rydyn ni wedi ymrwymo i barhau i ddiweddaru'r Senedd hon ac i ymwneud â phob Aelod ar y mater hollbwysig hwn.

contributions.text_english: Trefnydd, I'd like to request a statement from the Cabinet Minister for Enterprise, Connectivity and Energy on the announcement that Milford Haven's Impala terminal is to cease its commercial operations at the end of this year. We must fully understand the implications of this announcement, including the scale of any job losses and the impact on the local economy. We also need further clarity on how the Welsh Government intends to support both the company and its workforce as this situation develops. These are highly skilled and valuable jobs, and every effort must be made to retain this expertise within the region and to safeguard future employment opportunities. In my view, losing such skills would be a significant blow to the local economy and, indeed, to the wider energy sector. Given the vulnerability of older people, those living in residential care and individuals with underlying health concerns, there are serious questions about the infection control measures, the availability of treatment, support for care providers and the steps being taken to prevent further outbreaks. Given the significant public concern and the potential implications for public health, I believe that this matter warrants an urgent statement at the earliest opportunity. Diolch.

Can I call for two statements today, please? The first is from the Cabinet Secretary for Enterprise, Connectivity and Energy in relation to the mobile network. Action has been taken in Scotland and England, and they've announced this week in Scotland a consultation on changing permitted development rights in order to address mobile black spots. Given the essential nature of a decent mobile signal now, Wales is falling behind with this important digital infrastructure. We clearly need some action here, and I would be grateful if we could have an update on what action the Welsh Government is taking.

Also, can I call for a statement from the Welsh Government Cabinet Secretary responsible for social justice and equality on the action being taken by the Welsh Government to address antisemitism in Wales? As we all know, tomorrow marks the third anniversary of those barbaric attacks by Hamas and Islamic Jihad terrorists against Israeli citizens. All of us have condemned those attacks, and what we need to make sure is that Wales is taking appropriate action to address the rise in antisemitism that we've seen in our country since.

One positive action that the previous Welsh Government took, of course, was to recognise the International Holocaust Remembrance Alliance's definition of antisemitism, and I'd be grateful if the Welsh Government could reaffirm its commitment to that definition so that we can be sure that the same action will be taken by this new Welsh Government as the previous one in terms of providing some leadership on that issue.

contributions.text_english:
Minister, can I please request a statement from the Cabinet Minister for health and social care on support for people living with Huntington's disease? Huntington's is a rare neurological condition where symptoms affect thinking and cognitive abilities, as well as movement and behaviour. Symptoms usually develop between the ages of 30 and 50, with life expectancy from diagnosis being just 20 years. Anyone who has a parent with a faulty gene has a one in two chance of having Huntington's themselves. It's a really complex condition, with people requiring support from a number of health and care professionals. There's also a considerable mental health burden, with people often caring for family members whilst worrying about potentially carrying the faulty gene themselves.

Guidance published by the previous Welsh Government makes clear that those with a neurological condition such as Huntington's disease should not be excluded from mental health services. Guidance also calls for co-ordination of care across services, professions and agencies. Too many people say the healthcare service they access does not, in fact, meet their needs. A statement from the Cabinet Minister setting out what action the Welsh Government is taking to ensure that people with this devastating disease get the mental health support that they need and have a health professional to co-ordinate their care would be greatly appreciated. Thank you.

contributions.text_english: Trefnydd, could I ask for a statement from the Cabinet Secretary for health and social care on the operation of the 'Listening to People' NHS complaints process? Constituents have raised concerns with me following their experience of pursuing complaints involving Betsi Cadwaladr University Health Board. Thank you.

contributions.text_english: Prynhawn da, Drefnydd. Can I ask for a statement, please, on radical reform of services for our care-experienced young people? Back in July 2023, we debated in the Senedd the Children, Young People and Education Committee's report on this subject. Of the committee's 12 radical recommendations, the then Government accepted just one, rejecting—amongst other things—making care experience a protected characteristic and placing corporate duties on a statutory level. In that debate the now Deputy First Minister shared my disappointment that the Government then said it wasn't sufficiently bold, brave or ambitious. So, given that situation, I'd be pleased to hear from Plaid Cymru exactly how they're going to incorporate these issues around radical reform. It hasn't been so far in your statement for government or in your manifesto, but you've had a busy time, so I'm hoping that there will be a focus now on ensuring that our care-experienced young people across Wales get the services that they deserve. Diolch yn fawr iawn.

I thank the Member for raising this issue. Clearly, you will be aware of Plaid Cymru's commitment in terms of what you've outlined. The Deputy Minister with responsibility for this has heard the comments that you have made this afternoon.

Removing profit from the care sector is an issue that we worked on during the co-operation agreement, and that legislation is now in place and we're moving towards implementation during this Senedd term. The previous Government did sign a statement in 2025. As a new Government, we do support the principle of creating a care system that is more focused on families, is based on rights, is trauma informed, is locally rooted and is ambitious for all children, whilst removing profit from childcare and ensuring that no young person leaves care and goes into homelessness also. contributions.text_english: Trefnydd, can I ask for a statement on the Government's plans for improving pre-application consultations for major energy infrastructure developments, including solar farms, windfarms, new pylons and substations? My constituents feel ignored and dismayed. They believe these applications are just tick-box exercises. They tell me that notices intended to inform them are put up in places where they cannot be seen. They say letters arrive so late they have no meaningful chance to respond. To them, it feels like they are being deliberately denied a voice in decisions that will affect their homes and communities. They say they are being treated like mushrooms: fed farmyard manure and kept in the dark. So, Trefnydd, will the Government make a statement on how it will improve pre-application consultations for major energy infrastructure developments and ensure that communities are genuinely heard? Diolch.

contributions.text_original: Diolch i'r Aelod am godi'r materion hyn. Mae yna ymrwymiad clir gan y Llywodraeth hon o ran ein bod ni'n datblygu strategaeth ynni genedlaethol sydd yn mynd i'r afael â'r heriau hyn ac sy'n cynnwys cymunedau yn lle gwneud pethau i gymunedau, sef un o'r pwyntiau y mae'r Aelod yn eu codi. contributions.text_english: Minister, may I first of all warmly welcome the Plaid Cymru Government's announcement last week regarding the additional £3.4 million for Powys health board to help to reduce waiting times? This investment will make a difference to patients in Powys, where a large number depend on accessing healthcare services across the border in England. Given the vital role that cross-border healthcare plays for people in Powys and along Offa's Dyke, can we have a statement on this, please?
contributions.text_original: Weinidog, a gaf i groesawu yn y lle cyntaf yn fawr iawn gyhoeddiad Llywodraeth Plaid Cymru yr wythnos diwethaf ynghylch y £3.4 miliwn ychwanegol i fwrdd iechyd Powys i helpu i leihau amseroedd aros? Fe fydd y buddsoddiad hwn yn gwneud gwahaniaeth i gleifion ym Mhowys, lle mae nifer fawr yn dibynnu ar gael mynediad at wasanaethau gofal iechyd ar draws y ffin yn Lloegr. O ystyried y rôl hanfodol y mae gofal iechyd trawsffiniol yn ei chwarae i bobl ym Mhowys ac ar hyd Clawdd Offa, a oes modd cael sylw ar hyn, os gwelwch yn dda?

contributions.text_english: I thank the Member for raising this issue. I'm pleased that you do welcome this important investment. contributions.text_original: Diolch am godi'r mater hwn. Rwy'n falch eich bod chi yn croesawu'r buddsoddiad pwysig hwnnw. contributions.text_english: Thank you. And finally, David Mills.
contributions.text_original: Diolch. Ac yn olaf, David Mills.

contributions.text_english:
Thank you, Deputy Presiding Officer. I'd like to ask for a statement from the Cabinet Minister for Rural Resilience and Sustainability on how the Welsh Government intends to turn the lessons from this summer's wildfires and the very real risk of flooding this autumn and winter into investment in rural communities such as those across Brycheiniog Tawe Nedd.

Research has highlighted that measures such as rewetting peatland and better land management can help prevent wildfires, while also slowing water run-off and reducing flood risk. Indeed, the Welsh Government has already committed more than £5 million to natural flood management this financial year. So, could we have a statement setting out how farmers and landowners will be supported to deliver landscape-scale resilience and whether the Welsh Government will use this opportunity to bring much-needed investment and jobs into rural communities like mine?

contributions.text_english: Thank you, Trefnydd.
contributions.text_original: Diolch yn fawr iawn i chi, Drefnydd.

contributions.text_english: The next item is a statement by the Deputy Minister for Transport: strategic priorities for the Menai strait crossings and the M4 around Newport. I call on the Deputy Minister for Transport, Mark Hooper.
contributions.text_original: Nesaf, datganiad gan y Dirprwy Weinidog dros Drafnidiaeth: blaenoriaethau strategol ar gyfer croesfannau'r Fenai a'r M4 o amgylch Casnewydd. Galwaf ar y Dirprwy Weinidog dros Drafnidiaeth, Mark Hooper.

contributions.text_english: Dirprwy Lywydd, today I would like to set out the next steps for the Menai crossings and the M4 around Newport. We have agreed a way forward.
contributions.text_original: Dirprwy Lywydd, heddiw hoffwn nodi’r camau nesaf ar gyfer croesfannau'r Fenai a’r M4 o amgylch Casnewydd. Rydym wedi cytuno ar y ffordd ymlaen.

contributions.text_english:
The challenges on these routes are not new. They affect communities, businesses and travellers every day. The reviews we commissioned at the start of the summer were not about repeating decades of work explaining the problems, they were intended to identify a practical way forward. They have given us a clear direction. Today I am announcing action to develop a third Menai crossing and action to develop roads-based and engineering solutions for the M4 around Newport, alongside a programme of improvements that will help people and businesses while that work progresses.

Dirprwy Lywydd, people on Ynys Môn and across the north of our country know how disruptive it can be when one of the Menai crossings is restricted or closed. The review confirms that resilience remains the key challenge. That is why this Government will immediately recommence development work for a third Menai crossing. This will include design development, environmental assessment, business case preparation and the statutory processes needed to establish a deliverable scheme.

People have waited a long time for certainty about the future of the crossings. Today we are providing that direction. A third crossing remains the most effective option for improving resilience and providing additional capacity across the Menai strait. But major infrastructure cannot be delivered simply by announcing it. The necessary development work must be undertaken if we are to move from aspiration to a proposal that, ultimately, can be developed.

Alongside this work, we will continue investing in the infrastructure that we already have. We will maintain and operate both existing crossings to keep them safe and reliable. We will continue investment in targeted resilience measures on Britannia bridge, including wind deflectors, variable speed limits and other operational improvements designed to reduce disruption and keep traffic moving during challenging conditions. These measures will not replace the need for a third crossing. They will help improve resilience while development work on the third crossing progresses.

The review also examined three-lane tidal flow operation on Britannia bridge. The evidence identified significant safety and operational concerns and does not support taking this option forward.

Dirprwy Lywydd, turning now to the M4 around Newport: this is one of the most important transport corridors in Wales. Every day, thousands of people and businesses rely on this route to get to work, move goods and connect with customers, communities and ports across Wales. Yet, congestion continues to cause unreliable journeys and disruption that can quickly spread across the wider network. The review is clear that doing nothing is not an option. It also shows there is no single short-term intervention capable of solving the problem on its own. That is why this Welsh Government will now begin an 18-month programme of work to develop roads-based and engineering solutions for the M4 around Newport. This programme will consider a range of roads-based and engineering interventions and will identify a preferred option capable of providing a long-term response to the challenges on this route.

contributions.text_english:
Many people will understandably say that this issue has been debated for decades. They are right. But this work is not about revisiting old arguments. It is about developing options against current policy, environmental requirements, planning considerations and future travel demands, so that decisions can be taken on the basis of robust evidence and a clear understanding of what can realistically be delivered. Our objective is straightforward: we need a solution that is affordable, deliverable and capable of attracting the support and investment needed to make it happen. Without undertaking this work, there can be no credible pathway towards delivering future roads-based and engineering solutions.

But while this work progresses, we cannot simply wait. That is why we are also announcing a programme of improvements over the next five years. We will invest in the maintenance and renewal of the existing motorway and strategic road network. Over many years, Governments have often faced a choice between accepting disruption now or delaying important work until later. Understandably, there has often been a desire to minimise disruption in the short term, but that can make long-term challenges harder to address. Key infrastructure now requires significant renewal and maintenance work. I want to be honest: there will be periods of disruption while this work takes place. Nobody wants roadworks. Nobody enjoys delays. But continuing to defer this work will only lead to greater disruption and cost in the future. This Government is choosing to deal with that problem now.

We will also implement a five-year delivery plan, focused on practical improvements that people will start to see over the next two to three years, with further benefits building over time. This will include improvements to the way the motorway is operated and managed, including targeted improvements to roads and junctions, including potential closures, in and around Newport to improve traffic flow and resilience. The review found that measures such as these offer some of the quickest opportunities to improve traffic flow and resilience in the M4.

But we also recognise that changes affecting the motorway can have consequences for local roads. We will therefore work closely with Newport City Council, local communities and Members to develop these interventions so that the local impacts are properly considered alongside the benefits to the M4. At the same time, we will introduce measures to improve freight resilience by making better use of alternative routes such as the A465. This will maximise the investment made in the A465, supporting the provision of facilities that HGV drivers deserve, and at the same time alleviating pressure on the M4.

We will also continue investing in public transport, making it easier for more people to choose rail and bus services for everyday journeys between Newport and Cardiff, across the wider M4 corridor, and onwards into the rest of Wales and into England. The UK Government has committed to funding the rail stations recommended by the South East Wales Transport Commission. Last week I attended the joint UK-Welsh Government Wales rail board to discuss how we can accelerate delivery. I am pleased that Network Rail have committed to work collaboratively with Transport for Wales to draw on the expertise of both organisations, and TfW will take a direct role in constructing the stations.

We are setting up a new network south-east Wales board to oversee delivery. I have asked the team to prioritise delivery of the Cardiff parkway and Magor and Undy stations, so that communities can begin to benefit from these investments as soon as possible. We will also seek to improve access to Severn Tunnel Junction railway station and support improvements to bus connectivity between Newport and Cardiff, giving real options for travellers.

Dirprwy Lywydd, for too long, people and businesses have seen congestion around Newport become an accepted part of everyday life. This Government is choosing to act. The programme we are taking forward could reduce peak-hour traffic by about one in 10 vehicles. On a motorway that is already operating at or above capacity at the busiest times, that matters. It is a meaningful improvement over doing nothing and simply accepting increasing congestion on the network. But what matters is what these improvements mean in practice for people using the network every day. It means better travel choices through improved rail and bus services. It means the network is better able to cope when incidents occur, reducing the risk of small problems becoming major disruption. These are practical improvements that people should begin to notice in their everyday lives over the coming years.

Dirprwy Lywydd, people want action, not endless discussion. They want government to deal with today's challenges while properly planning for the future. That is exactly what we are doing. At the Menai strait, we are getting on with the work needed to develop a third crossing whilst managing resilience now. Around Newport, we are developing long-term road space and engineering solutions for the M4 whilst delivering practical improvements over the next five years. These are major transport challenges that have built up over many years; they will not be resolved overnight. But, today, we are providing a clear direction, taking practical actions now and developing the longer-term solutions needed for the future.

contributions.text_original: Ddirprwy Lywydd, rydym yn gweithredu nawr. Rydym yn cyflawni gwelliannau dros y bum mlynedd nesaf ac yn datblygu atebion ar gyfer ein dyfodol. Diolch yn fawr.

contributions.text_english:
Oh dear, oh dear, oh dear, Minister. We were expecting a lot more on this side of the Chamber. But, anyway, we'll start north and then we'll travel south, if that's okay.

So, I'll start with the positives. Nice to see we're doing some baby steps with the current bridges that cross the Menai strait. Wind deflectors—let's get on with that as soon as we can, improve those; we've got a winter ahead of us. And varying the speed limit—we like varying the speed limit in this Chamber, don't we—I'll give you a positive on that one. But, in terms of the actual third bridge, it sounds like you're just thinking about a third bridge, which simply is not good enough. So, you're going to recommence development work and look at design development, environmental assessment, business case preparation. To me, it doesn't sound like you're completely committed to a third crossing, because I thought we'd done all this work before. I thought this was called the purple route and that that work had been done. And obviously what's disappointing to see, and this is why I question your commitment, is there's nothing in here about funding a third bridge. It's going to be an expensive project and is going to need cross-party support, and there's nothing in here about that. So, I want to ask you, and you can answer once I've finished, clearly: are you actually committed to building the third bridge across the Menai strait, 'yes' or 'no'?

Right, then, let's head down south. Now you need more thinking time—18 months of more thinking time—about solutions. And again, I thought we'd been here and gone through all of that with the M4 relief road and the black route. And in between the thinking time—which you clearly need, fair enough—for the next five years, you're going to do some improvements, which, personally, I think is just a sticking-plaster approach that ties in directly to Plaid Cymru's anti-motorist stance.

Let's talk about closing junctions. I do love the statistic about one in 10 cars not making it onto the M4. Of course they can't make it onto the M4, because they can't get onto the M4 because you've closed the junction. Closing junctions doesn't solve congestion and it's going to move that onto Newport's local roads. Newport City Council recently—July 2026—voted unanimously against any measure that diverts traffic onto Newport's already congested streets. I don't think they will be so delighted with your statement today. As we in Reform have said, stopping cars getting onto the motorway isn't a solution that Newport will thank you for. And in your own assessment, the cost of this is £14 million, and reducing traffic by a whopping 3 per cent.

Let's go over to the Heads of the Valleys plan. So, let me just get this right: ferries transport comes off the boats in Pembroke and then goes across east to Dover and on to Europe, and what you want to do is encourage, persuade, divert that freight traffic to go up over the Heads of the Valleys and back down again, and the cost of doing that is £49 million, which is some pretty swanky cafes and some nice rest facilities, and you think that will reduce the traffic on the M4 by 1 per cent. It's just not going to happen.

And then, finally, we get on to rail. Now, let's be clear: Reform supports more rail capacity, but rail should add choice, not be used to justify restricting road access. As Laura Anne Jones pointed out, the M4 users have no realistic alternative. We need to remind ourselves that, unlike us, there are a lot of people who aren't members of the lanyard class who go to work each day with a small briefcase. How are delivery drivers and tradespeople going to get on the train? 'Excuse me, ma'am, can you just move to one side while I put my 12 pots of paint and my toolbox there?' It's not going to happen.

Basically, Minister, I'm asking you to drop your ideology. What you've done here is pretend to be committed to fixing the road issues, but actually you're thinking about a bridge, you've got 18 months more of thinking about the M4, and you've got a five-year scheme, which, essentially, is going to cost millions of pounds and reduce traffic congestion by 4 per cent. So, here is the solution. On your last page of your statement, you say, 'We are developing a long-term roads-based and engineering solution.' Well, I'll tell you, we've got one: it's the M4 relief road, the black route. Reform UK have costed this at £2.8 billion. Yes, that's a lot of money, but I will guarantee here that, if there is a Reform Welsh Government, we will be lobbying and working with a Reform UK Westminster Government—which is coming, ladies and gentlemen—and we will build the M4 relief road. So, Minister, I want to confirm: are you committed to the bridge, completely and utterly committed? And please stop thinking and just get on with it. Diolch yn fawr.

Yes, that's a lot of money, but I will guarantee here that, if there is a Reform Welsh Government, we will be lobbying and working with a Reform UK Westminster Government—which is coming, ladies and gentlemen—and we will build the M4 relief road. Thank you for the question. Before I answer, I just want to thank those Members who turned up for the briefing with officials this morning, and also subsequent conversations in this regard. It was a shame that Members from Reform chose not to undertake those conversations. There were specific conversations that were not entered into, and that was a real shame, because that would have given them the chance to have understood some of the detail behind this more clearly.

In answer to the questions on Menai, I don't think the Member, frankly, understands the process you need to go through to build. This is a significant piece of engineering. It is appropriate that we do it in the phases that we say we are. To be clear, this Government is committed to delivering a third crossing across the Menai. There are no ifs, no buts. That is absolutely clear. What you have to do to do that is to take stages. Now, the Member, and all of this group around here, just seem to think that you can click a finger and things happen. Let's get into the real world. The real world is that it takes real work to get these things done. The interesting thing is, when I was speaking to civil servants earlier prior to this, I was saying I was looking forward to this debate, because I do look forward to these debates. Do you know what they were saying? They're looking forward to getting stuck in to doing the work. That's what they're waiting for, and that's what's going to happen. What's happened for too long is this body politic has failed to deliver. If we have conversations that are in the style that we've had today, we'll continue to do that. But the rest of the Siambr, hopefully, will focus on getting things done. Because if you're just going to backbite on that, it helps nobody, frankly.

Turning to the M4, I think this is a real misunderstanding as well of what a 10 per cent change will do on the M4 with the plan of action that we've put together. Ten per cent—. And I'm sure that Members opposite me as well are probably thinking, 'I wish we'd done some more of this 10 per cent.' But, over the past 27 years, there's been very limited change on the M4. This Government is committing itself, over the next five years, to making an actual difference to people. And 3 per cent here and 1 per cent there makes a real difference. This is about a strategic suite of projects that need to be deployed together. These are the ways that we make the difference to the M4. And it's not straightforward. There is no silver bullet. If there was, we'd talk about it. You talk about the black route as if it's deliverable. That went when it was cancelled. The protected route status went when it was cancelled. So, we're talking about decades of work to even get that off the ground. So, to suggest to the people outside that you can deliver it in an instant is disingenuous—and I'm being kind in saying that.

In terms of the A465—. There are a lot of questions to get through, I will try and be—. But, in terms of the A465, unlike you I've actually spoken to hauliers, who see this as a realistic option. But the haulage companies are looking for facilities, because, unlike some parts of Europe where they actually invest in facilities for drivers—. Drivers are professional. Across the UK, we have very, very poor facilities. This Government is going to make a difference to that, and we've had support from across the industry to say that they want to see those facilities. That will direct people across the piece, and that's including people from Ireland as well as haulage companies from the UK.

Rail adding choice and taking people off the motorway—. One of the things about adding choice using rail is exactly what you just said, it takes people—. So, I may be taking a car; I can now use the rail. That frees up space on the motorway for those people who need to use the motorway in the way that you described. It's a practical way of making a difference. The sad thing is that the Burns review—. I can just hear muttering behind me. Do you want to make an intervention or not?

contributions.text_english:
I thank the Deputy Minister for his statement. After 30 talking shops, reviews and expert panels in the Government's first 100 days, I was hoping for something different from you today. I'm sorry to say I've been rather disappointed.

Now, progress on that third Menai crossing is very welcome. It builds on the work that Welsh Labour had undertaken in Government. But families in Newport will feel let down that, rather than acting now, the Government is launching yet another review on the M4, and we won't have any answers for 18 months. So, my first question to you today, Minister, is: why will it take that long to come up with some serious road-based answers for traffic around Newport? Aren't you just kicking the can down the road and hoping that families in Newport won't notice? And Deputy Minister, if you'd spoken to people in Newport, we think you wouldn't need that long. You'd have been told unequivocally that junction closures will bring more traffic and more air pollution, that silent killer, into the hearts and lungs of communities.

In Government, Welsh Labour took action to help alleviate congestion on the M4 around Newport. We'd secured funding for new railway stations from the UK Labour Government as part of that generational £14 billion commitment to transform rail infrastructure in Wales. We completed the Heads of the Valleys A465 road, the biggest road building scheme in Europe, offering traffic from the north and Midlands an alternative route into south Wales. So, I do welcome your proposals to increase the level of haulage traffic there.

We also commissioned independent evidence-based resilience studies, not just of the M4, but the A55, the A494 and the A483 to ensure that roads are fit for the future. Those resilience studies are vital work that should form the basis of future recommendations, but they appear now to be gathering dust on the Government's shelves, with no comment today on the A484 or the A483 or the A55 east of the Menai strait, where you'll know that there are significant traffic problems. Deputy Minister, as you know, Welsh Labour's view is that devolution shouldn't stop at Cardiff Bay, that Wales is too centralised, and local leaders should have a far greater say on the issues that affect their communities, and this decision today is a case in point: trunk roads are maintained and owned by the Welsh Government, but they should be designed and delivered for the regions and economies that they serve. So, will you commit to engaging fully with families, drivers, businesses and local leaders in Newport before any decision is taken about junction closures? Will you also commit to publishing the evidence behind any junction closures in full? And finally, will you also commit the Government to publishing a full response to those resilience reviews that Welsh Labour started in Government?

I really appreciate the question, and I think, despite the disappointment that was expressed in that statement, there were a lot of things that you agreed with, so I welcome that. I'll deal with junction closures at the end, if I may. The resilience studies, in the first instance, that you asked about, when they're ready to be published, I'll be publishing them. They'll be published in full. I think there's good work that's being undertaken, and it does feed into the wider issues across Wales. One thing I've been really committed to is that there were two issues of strategic importance when I came into office: one was around Menai, and one was around the M4. So, I focused very much on those, and asked for the resources to be put into that thinking, in the first instance, to make sure we got those right.

In terms of 18 months, 18 months is actually a relatively fast time period to get the sort of work that we want to do done, but whilst those 18 months are happening, this Government isn't standing still. We've designed and put together a package, a full range of interventions, that need to be seen as a whole, not just my interventions in and of themselves. Some of them will be relatively easy. It will be relatively easy to direct people along the A465. Some of them are trickier. Some of them will require—. Like you said, the UK Government committed the £14 billion, it needs to show us the money on that. That's the next stage of this now, so that the work can be done.

I referenced in my statement that Transport for Wales would be working on developing those stations. That's a massive change of heart from UK Government that shows the positive relationship we've had with the Department for Transport and with Network Rail, that they see what Transport for Wales have done on the core Valleys lines and want to be able to utilise that same workforce. Remember that's a Welsh workforce developing, so the economy benefits from that work.

You asked a specific question, whether or not I commit to working with the communities of Newport and wider with regard to publishing the data around junction closures. The answer is a very emphatic 'yes' on that. One of the things that we need to do is to make sure that people don't feel like there are things being done to them. We want to work with Newport City Council and the other councils that also interact with these junctions as well. So, I give my commitment and the commitment of the teams who are working on this to do that. That's probably the most important thing about this. We're trying to make sure that this process has been transparent. That's the reason we're publishing the report that was issued today. You will all have had it in your inboxes. This isn't something that's being held behind closed doors. We didn't put a Lord's name on it. We've taken responsibility ourselves to move this thing forward. So, I'm really keen to continue this engagement to make sure that we get it right.

contributions.text_english:
Before I begin my contribution, I just want to thank the Minister for the meeting that we had this morning. It was incredibly productive, and also I'm delighted for the residents and activists of the Magor and Undy station who have been campaigning for decades. It has been a labour of love to get that station going. So, I am really pleased that we're heading in the right direction. I know it's been something that we've worked on for years and years and years, and I know they will be delighted with the response.

So, Deputy Minister, I wholeheartedly agree with you that something needs to be done when it comes to improving the M4 around Newport, but this is not the right way. Not a day goes by when drivers, many of them my constituents, aren't caught up in traffic along the M4 at Newport. Bumper-to-bumper traffic regularly plagues that important stretch of road, causing frustration and making Wales a less attractive place to do business. You could have brought that to an end today, Deputy Minister, but instead you seem hell-bent on making things 100 times worse by closing junctions along the M4. A full closure at junction 27 at High Cross, a partial closure of junction 26 at Malpas, and a partial closure of junction 25 at Caerleon will cause complete chaos across the city. How on earth have you come to the conclusion that this will help improve the situation? All it is going to do is clog up Newport's surrounding A roads and residential streets.

Deputy Minister, do you not accept that your decision is going to have a major impact on commuters and businesses, both of which our city's economy relies on? And how were these junctions identified? Did you carry out an impact assessment before reaching this decision? If so, will you commit to publishing the findings in full? And if not, why not? I'd like to know what conversations you've had with residents, businesses, the police, the ambulance service, the city council and other key stakeholders about these junction closure plans. I cannot stress enough how much of a backward step this, Deputy Minister. By even considering junction closures, you have consigned Newport to even more misery.

Let me take you back a few years, Deputy Minister. Former transport Minister Edwina Hart pushed ahead with closing junction 41 on the M4 in Port Talbot during rush-hour times back in 2014. Sound familiar, Minister? Her plans were quickly abandoned following huge public backlash from traders in the area reporting a 20 per cent drop in business and long-standing businesses closing for good. So, before you resign yourself to repeating the same mistakes as Edwina, have you carried out any modelling on the economic damage this is going to cause to Newport? After 27 years of Labour's failures, the people of Newport cannot afford any more blunders being made by Plaid Cymru. Whilst I believe junction closures should be an absolute non-starter from the get-go, will you be monitoring the effectiveness of these closures and will this evidence be reviewed? If these closures do not do what you think they will do, will you commit to reopening these vital junctions?

The junction closures form part of a wider package of proposed measures, many of which, I'm sure you'll be pleased to hear, I do actually support. A commitment to investing in the extra road network, accelerating plans to deliver railway stations and improve rest stops for HGV drivers, are very welcome in my book. But I want to touch upon the plans for freight, with your ambition for redirecting HGVs away from the M4 and onto the Heads of the Valleys road. This stretch of road currently runs at 50 mph, so will you be looking to increase the speed limit to 70 mph as a result of the anticipated influx? What discussions have you had with the hauliers and others about these plans and what has the response been like? I'd really like to know.

My Welsh Conservative colleagues and I have been very, very clear that the best way of unblocking the M4 is via a relief road. Without a relief road, Newport and the rest of south Wales will continue to see more delays, more congestion, more disruption and more damage to the Welsh economy. So, as part of your long-term plans, will you commit to making sure an M4 relief road will be firmly back on the agenda?

I'd also like to know what other sorts of options are on the cards. Will you be open to considering tunnel widening, as I have previously raised with you here in the Chamber? When will this piece of work get under way and when can we expect a final decision to be reached? Deputy Minister, I appreciate funding for the stations is a matter for Westminster, but can you share with us the total anticipated cost of the five-year plans and how they will be met?

Whilst it is a bit of doom and gloom here in the south of Wales with your transport plans, things seem to be looking a bit brighter in the north. My Welsh Conservative colleagues and I have long called for a third Menai crossing to be built, so we are actually delighted to see this important infrastructure project set to be delivered. In particular, I know my colleague Janet Finch-Saunders will be thrilled with today's announcement. The public meeting held by Janet on a third crossing demonstrated not only significant cross-party support, but also overwhelming support from members of the public who were in attendance. More than 1,000 people signed a petition calling for a third Menai crossing within just 24 hours. That's pretty impressive.

We cannot deny that the Menai crossings are indeed essential access points on and off Anglesey, as well as a main artery for people and businesses travelling to and from Holyhead—as well as the port—including those travelling to Ireland. With 50,000 vehicles crossing the Menai and Britannia bridges each day, these crossings are vital for residents, businesses, tourism and the wider north Wales economy. Yet we have seen just how fragile these are, with the Menai bridge closing in October 2025 for repair work and the problems that have indeed followed. These closures, as I'm sure we're all aware, have caused significant impact, causing delays, congestion and disruption for residents, visitors and businesses. So, Deputy Minister, when will we expect to see spades in the ground and work under way to build this vital third crossing?

Details on the cost of the project and timelines would be greatly appreciated, and in terms of the existing Menai bridge, are the repair works still on course to be completed early next year? And on that note, Deputy Minister, what further steps will the Welsh Government be taking to increase the resilience of the two existing crossings? As much as I could continue on these important topics, Deputy Presiding Officer, I will draw my remarks to a close, as I appreciate there's a lot to unpack there. Thank you.

So, as part of your long-term plans, will you commit to making sure an M4 relief road will be firmly back on the agenda?

I'd also like to know what other sorts of options are on the cards. Will you be open to considering tunnel widening, as I have previously raised with you here in the Chamber? When will this piece of work get under way and when can we expect a final decision to be reached? Deputy Minister, I appreciate funding for the stations is a matter for Westminster, but can you share with us the total anticipated cost of the five-year plans and how they will be met?

Whilst it is a bit of doom and gloom here in the south of Wales with your transport plans, things seem to be looking a bit brighter in the north. My Welsh Conservative colleagues and I have long called for a third Menai crossing to be built, so we are actually delighted to see this important infrastructure project set to be delivered. In particular, I know my colleague Janet Finch-Saunders will be thrilled with today's announcement. The public meeting held by Janet on a third crossing demonstrated not only significant cross-party support, but also overwhelming support from members of the public who were in attendance. More than 1,000 people signed a petition calling for a third Menai crossing within just 24 hours. That's pretty impressive.

We cannot deny that the Menai crossings are indeed essential access points on and off Anglesey, as well as a main artery for people and businesses travelling to and from Holyhead—as well as the port—including those travelling to Ireland. With 50,000 vehicles crossing the Menai and Britannia bridges each day, these crossings are vital for residents, businesses, tourism and the wider north Wales economy. Yet we have seen just how fragile these are, with the Menai bridge closing in October 2025 for repair work and the problems that have indeed followed. These closures, as I'm sure we're all aware, have caused significant impact, causing delays, congestion and disruption for residents, visitors and businesses. So, Deputy Minister, when will we expect to see spades in the ground and work under way to build this vital third crossing?

Details on the cost of the project and timelines would be greatly appreciated, and in terms of the existing Menai bridge, are the repair works still on course to be completed early next year? And on that note, Deputy Minister, what further steps will the Welsh Government be taking to increase the resilience of the two existing crossings? As much as I could continue on these important topics, Deputy Presiding Officer, I will draw my remarks to a close, as I appreciate there's a lot to unpack there. Thank you.

And, again, thank you for the constructive way you approached the conversation this morning. I do appreciate it. And I think the frankness—. I didn't expect agreements as you walked into the Siambr today to talk about this, but I think what we got was a situation of understanding some of the issues that we're addressing.

I think, when we talk about junction closures, the thing that I'm really clear about is that it's something where I do recognise the concerns that are out there, and this is something that is very, very important that we get right. So, as I said in my answer to Vikki just a few minutes ago, I'm committed to engaging not just with Newport City Council and the surrounding councils, but with traders and local communities to make sure we understand how things can be mitigated and how things can work better as well. The three junctions you're talking about, one of them is a full closure, whereas the other ones will see changes that are less severe. So, it's about understanding the impacts of each one, which will be quite different.

The other thing I think is important to note is that we talk about this as if the intra-Newport system is working well, and, frankly, it isn't. Whereas I've got responsibility for the strategic road network, this is about working with Newport City Council, together, and the corporate joint committee as well, to make sure that we're delivering across the piece to improve the whole thing. The M4 is part of the system that makes Newport work, or not at the moment, and we've got to improve that. It's a youthful city, and people are expecting a modern city with modern public transport facilities. But at the moment, today, it's the most car-dependent city in Wales. So, we've got to do things to give people the choice. And going back to the point I made earlier, that choice needs to be very real and needs to be effective.

On the A465, we've had discussions with hauliers; we'll have more discussions with hauliers. But the initial points were to be welcomed, particularly about the routes that we're talking about from Fishguard into the midlands. It's a perfect route for that, but currently, it's not being chosen as the route of choice, and part of that is about providing the facilities. At the moment, we have freight drivers who are having to park in car parks and lay-bys, and it's wholly inappropriate. This is something that we can make a definite difference on and can attract drivers onto that route again. And again, going back to every time we take some of that traffic off the M4, it frees up space for people who have no choice but to use the M4.

Tunnel widening was one of the points that was considered in this review. I would imagine that it'll be considered within the 18-month review as well, with more detail. But at this point in time, it was considered it wasn't something where we had a route to take forward at the moment. The timescales associated with the disruption are something like 12 years before it gets finished. So, it's something that we'll look at in more detail. And on that point, I'd encourage Members from across the piece to engage in that piece of work, to make sure that they find out what's going on, and I'll do my best to make sure that Members are appraised of it, as we go through.

In terms of the Menai and when it happens, there is a process that you need to go through to be able to get a bridge to start. We're making a commitment that we want this bridge to be built. I think I've made that clear. That process starts today. That process then goes through—. There are a number of stages to it. What I'll be doing is updating this Siambr with written statements to talk about how that progress happens. The major work on a bridge build happens in the latter end of that, after all the plans have been approved, and all the environmental regulations, et cetera, have been agreed to. So, you'll see the actual spades in the ground, but the real work, and a lot of the work, will start now. That work starts now. So, we're looking at somewhere between eight and 10 years for that bridge to be finished and to be opened. That's a realistic timetable. And as I hope Members will understand, I'd rather deal with realism, rather than deal with things that won't happen, which brings me to the black route.

This is a project now—. There is no deliverable opportunity for the black route. So, I would encourage the Members opposite, and other Members in the Siambr, just to think about what we can do to make practical improvements today. Because my concern is—and I've said this before—the body politic has let people down in Newport, and outside, by not solving these issues. So, there are lots of things you agree with, and I'm glad for that support.

Thank you, Deputy Minister, for today's announcement. People on both sides of the Menai strait will judge this statement on whether it gives them a credible plan that's both affordable and keeps traffic moving. When either of the existing bridges fail, hospital appointments are missed, staff are late for work, and businesses in Bangor and on Ynys Môn lose trade. Local estimates put that at £30 million a year. So, we welcome this announcement.

But given how tight Welsh budgets are, and that we're already suffering under unbearable taxes, I worry how we can afford this. Given Holyhead's role as the principal gateway between Great Britain and Ireland, can the Deputy Minister please tell us: has he appealed for funding for the third bridge from the UK Government, and, if so, how have they responded? Are they prepared to pick up the lion's share of this bill? And if the UK Government does not share the bill, how will the Welsh Government finance the £400 million to £600 million cost? Thank you.

Thank you for the question. I think the Member is jumping one step ahead, but it's an important question to start addressing, and it is front of our mind as well. You asked whether it's a credible plan. That's why we're making the steps today, so that people can understand that this is a credible plan. We are committed to the third Menai crossing, so the plan will be something that is very deliverable.

When it comes to financing it, this is part of the work that we would need to do. The Member makes a good point that the Menai strait is a link between us and Europe, through Holyhead. It's the second-biggest roll-on, roll-off ferry terminal in the country, so the benefit of that is really important. The other infrastructure projects that are happening on the island equally need a crossing that's going to be sustainable. So, discussions with the UK Government will have to occur with this. There are ways of being able to fund this. The plans are already starting to be put into place, but I'll be coming back with future plans as this work progresses.

This statement is telling us what we already know: that there is a problem on the M4 around Newport. It really is astounding that junction closures are even being considered as part of the solution by this Plaid Cymru Government. The people of Newport are not to blame for the congestion on the M4. The motorway runs through the city, and whenever there's an accident or a major event, traffic shifts onto local roads, grinding Newport to a halt.

Local people, including in surrounding areas like Risca, Blackwood and Cwmbran, need to have their voices heard, and people haven't been involved at this point. These people aren't just data points in a transport policy document; they are individuals, families and businesses whose lives will be impacted. They should be at the heart of this Government's approach to the M4. But local people's voices are clear: fully closing the junction at High Cross and the eastbound junctions at Malpas and Caerleon will bring more traffic and air pollution closer to homes, schools and businesses—

contributions.text_english: Thank you for your statement, Deputy Minister, on the M4 relief road in particular. Can I ask two things? First, you talked about disruption while this work is ongoing. What level of disruption are motorists going to have to endure? Because at the moment the road is gridlocked most days and, at its worst, it can be gridlocked back to the Severn bridge, or to Cardiff Gate if you're travelling east. So, any potential disruption is going to have a devastating impact. And secondly, the really important thing here is capacity. The issue you've got here is that the modelling that was done for the inquiry into the black route showed an 18 per cent growth rate in traffic over 15 years. You've talked of a 10 per cent reduction. That's still an 8 per cent growth in traffic using the M4 as it's currently constructed, or as you've outlined today. The real issue here is not the failure of body politic, as you put it, to agree the solution; it's the Labour Party supported by your party's refusal to build the black route. Because if we had the black route, that capacity would be there and the economy of south Wales and the wider region would be doing so much better.

Can I help the Member with the second part of that question? The 10 per cent improvement was in 2042 expected traffic volumes. So, it's a 10 per cent improvement on them, which has built some of those increases before. So, it does make a valid and important difference. Is it enough? I don't think it is, which is the reason we've got this 18-month piece of work as well to look at other longer term solutions alongside this. But the point is we're not going to stop.

You talked about disruption, and I think this is a really important point, so thank you for raising it. For too long, the M4 and the rest of our strategic road network hasn't been maintained in the manner that it should have been. Maintaining a network is like maintaining a boiler at home. It needs to be serviced. If you don't service it when it does work, the problems manifest. We want to make sure that we grasp that and deal with these issues. It's also a serious thing that we do. I'm hopeful that we get broad support so that we solve and maintain our networks as we should. It's one of our biggest assets on our balance sheet.

The M4 runs through my constituency. Communities across Newport and beyond feel the impact of congestion every single day. These problems are not new. Successive Labour Government have had 27 years to act. They commissioned studies, gathered the evidence and spent more than £150 million developing the M4 relief road only for it ultimately to be abandoned with a promise of other solutions.

But the reality is Newport has been left without a solution, yet these same voices are now very vocal when this Welsh Government is grasping the nettle. So, the question is: will these proposals solve the problem? Time will tell, and I will continue to scrutinise the Government on these solutions. But one thing is clear: doing nothing is not an option.

I welcome the commitment to work with Newport City Council and other local government partners while ensuring residents and businesses have a meaningful voice. So, Minister, how will you sequence and implement these proposals over the next 18 months and ensure that local government, residents and businesses genuinely shape the decisions that you take? Diolch yn fawr.

Deputy Minister, much of what I'm going to say some people have already asked, so I'll try to skirt around the edges. These words aren't mine, but those of my residents within Newport. They're deeply concerned by reports that your Government is considering closing M4 junctions around our city. Local commuters have warned that this would mean turning local roads and school routes into highway relief tracks, forcing motorway traffic off the M4 into residential streets, where families live and children travel to and from every day. The lack of an overall system basis taking into account flows from junction 23 to junction 28 is short-sighted. We seem to fixate on junction 25 onwards, but it starts before then. It will lead to continued use of the well-known runs to divert around any issues that happen on the M4, whether Brynglas or accident related.

There are also serious concerns for Newport's economy. Small and medium-sized businesses are already operating in challenging conditions, and restricting motorway access risks making it harder for customers, employees and suppliers to reach their destinations. Will the Minister rule out closure of M4 junctions if the public's voice says that they oppose it and commit to solutions that reduce congestion without putting children, communities and the local economy at greater risk?

contributions.text_english:
Thank you, Dirprwy Lywydd. Safeguarding is one of the most fundamentally important responsibilities of any government. It's about ensuring that all children, young people and adults who are at risk have the right to live their lives safe from abuse, neglect, exploitation or harm. That is why safeguarding remains a key priority for this Government, and that is why strengthening safeguarding arrangements is central to our programme for government.

Today, I'm announcing 'Stronger Safeguarding for a Safer Wales', the Welsh Government's whole-system safeguarding improvement programme for this Senedd term. The programme brings together our work to strengthen safeguarding arrangements for children, young people and adults who are facing risk, and does so under a single improvement framework. It recognises that while safeguarding responsibilities might differ across services and sectors, there is a need for effective leadership, intelligence, accountability, learning and lived experience to be at the heart of the whole safeguarding system.

Recently, safeguarding reviews, inspections, inquiries and practice reviews have demonstrated the strengths of our safeguarding arrangements, as well as the devastating consequences when those arrangements fail. At the same time, the risks that people face continue to evolve. New forms of exploitation are emerging. Public expectations are rising, and rightly so. The systems designed to protect people must continue to adapt and improve.

Mae'n golygu gwneud yn siŵr bod gan bob plentyn, pob person ifanc a phob oedolyn sy’n wynebu risg yr hawl i fyw eu bywydau'n ddiogel rhag camdriniaeth, esgeulustod, camfanteisio neu niwed. Dyna pam mae diogelu yn dal i fod yn flaenoriaeth allweddol i'r Llywodraeth hon, a dyna pam mae cryfhau trefniadau diogelu yn ganolog i'n rhaglen lywodraethu.

Heddiw, dwi'n cyhoeddi 'Diogelu Cryfach ar gyfer Cymru Fwy Diogel', sef rhaglen Llywodraeth Cymru ar gyfer tymor y Senedd hon i wella trefniadau diogelu ar draws y system gyfan. Mae'r rhaglen yn dwyn ynghyd ein gwaith i gryfhau trefniadau diogelu ar gyfer plant, pobl ifanc ac oedolion sy’n wynebu risg, a hynny o dan un fframwaith gwella. contributions.text_english:
Our commitments are clear. Children's voices must be heard and must be acted on. The signs of abuse must be recognised earlier. Lessons have to be learned when safeguarding concerns arise, and we are committed to taking forward duties to report child sexual abuse. Those commitments remain central to our approach. This Government is clear that safeguarding cannot simply be an aspiration, it must be demonstrated through action. Every review provides lessons that must be learned. Every inspection identifies chances that might have been missed, opportunities for improvement. Every safeguarding incident demands reflection and action. But if we respond only to individual events, we risk creating a system that is reactive rather than preventative. Our ambition must be greater than that.

We need a safeguarding system that continuously learns, identifies risks earlier, shares intelligence effectively and acts before harm escalates. We need a safeguarding system that is joined up, accountable and ensures that lessons lead to consistent improvement across Wales. That is why the strengthening safeguarding governance review that was led by Jan Pickles has been so important and continues to be important. The review found that while Wales has strong legislative foundations, safeguarding governance has become fragmented, with inconsistent intelligence arrangements, limited national oversight and a need for clearer accountability.

The Cabinet Minister for Health and Care and I have accepted the recommendations from phase 1 of the review. The opportunity before us is not simply to implement individual recommendations, of course, it's an opportunity to strengthen the safeguarding system as a whole and ensure that it is equipped to respond to the risks of today and the challenges of the future. The stronger safeguarding for a safer Wales programme is designed to achieve that. It brings together our commitments, lessons learned and review findings together into a single programme of safeguarding reform. Its purpose is clear, as I've said: to strengthen leadership, to make the system more coherent, to promote the effectiveness of safeguarding and to ensure—and this is central, Deputy Llywydd—that the voices of children, young people, adults at risk, victims and survivors shape the services designed to protect them.

The programme is structured around four ambitions: stronger leadership and accountability for safeguarding; clear and consistent safeguarding arrangements throughout Wales; a system that learns and improves; and listening to children and adults and acting earlier. These ambitions will be delivered through a phased programme of activity across this Senedd term. Together, they'll create the foundations for improving the system over the long term.

contributions.text_english:
A key element of the programme will be the establishment of a ministerial safeguarding oversight and assurance board. This will strengthen national leadership, accountability and oversight of safeguarding risks across Wales, ensuring a clear line of sight between safeguarding intelligence, system performance and ministerial assurance.

We will establish a dedicated safeguarding function within a national social care intelligence hub. The hub will bring together intelligence, data, evidence and lessons from across Wales. It will strengthen our ability to identify emerging risks, understand patterns of harm and support more informed decision making across the safeguarding system. It will also help ensure that lessons from reviews, inspections and wider safeguarding activity are translated into action. We will also develop a national safeguarding plan and a national safeguarding risk register. Together, these will provide a clear national framework for safeguarding improvement, helping to align priorities, strengthen accountability and support greater consistency across Wales.

The programme will also create the conditions for future reform. And this will include our intention to consult on proposals for an adult and child protection authority for Wales, helping to inform the future shape of safeguarding arrangements in Wales. Alongside these developments, we will continue to take forward our commitment to strengthen duties to report child sexual abuse. This delivers on our manifesto commitment and builds upon the recommendations of the independent inquiry into child sexual abuse.

Children, young people, adults at risk, victims and survivors often have the clearest understanding of how safeguarding systems work in practice and where they need to improve. Their voices must never be an afterthought. They must be central to how safeguarding services are designed, scrutinised and improved. That's why lived experience will be embedded throughout this programme. The experiences of all victims and survivors will help shape that improvement, that accountability and those future developments of the system, because safeguarding systems should not simply work on paper. They should be shaped by the people they exist to protect.

Stronger safeguarding for a safer Wales is our commitment to creating the conditions for better protection, stronger accountability and improved outcomes for children, young people and adults at risk across Wales. We owe it to them to get this right. Diolch.

contributions.text_english:
Thank you, Deputy Minister. I welcome the statement and the recognition that safeguarding is one of the most important responsibilities of any Government. Every single one of us in this Chamber has been given the honour of representing the people of Wales, and with that honour there comes a strong responsibility to protect our most vulnerable and to challenge the system that fails them. However awkward the questions, however uncomfortable the answers, we must have the courage to act. Safeguarding is essential. Children, patients and adults at risk must be protected. People must feel confident about reporting concerns, knowing they will be heard and taken seriously.

I welcome the Minister's emphasis on strengthening safeguarding across Wales and on creating a system that is proactive rather than reactive, one that learns lessons and acts before harm escalates. But we must never judge safeguarding by what it achieves. A policy is only effective if it works in practice. Additional procedures must address and identify problems and deliver a clear benefit. We must distinguish between preventing abuse and investigating allegations against those entrusted with people's care. Both require accountability.

Children can face exploitation in their homes, their communities and online. They may not recognise the abuse. They may even defend the person harming them. Protection cannot depend on a child finding the words to explain what is happening. Warning signs must never be dismissed because an individual is respected, an organisation fears embarrassment or someone is uncomfortable asking difficult questions. That principle applies everywhere, including hospitals and care settings.

Proper scrutiny also demands fair treatment. Doctors, nurses, social care workers, teachers and foster carers carry enormous responsibilities. We want people to enter these roles, stay in them and feel supported to provide good care. An allegation must be taken seriously. It must never be treated as a verdict. Immediate protective action may be necessary while facts are established. The action must reflect the risk, being regularly reviewed and accompanied by a fair and timely investigation. Where a process becomes unnecessarily prolonged or poorly co-ordinated, the consequences of this can reach into someone's livelihood, family life, confidence and mental health. For a foster family, an investigation affects their home. For a nurse or a doctor, it can leave their professional future uncertain. Children, patients and those reporting harm also need answers. Avoidable delay serves nobody. When an investigation continues for months, who is responsible for its progress, who reviews the restrictions, who challenges the unnecessary delay? The statement speaks of stronger leadership and accountability. Those principles must apply not only when concerns are raised, but throughout the safeguarding process itself. Several bodies may have legitimate responsibilities, but there must be clear co-ordination with avoidable duplication identified and removed. Those affected need clear communication, appropriate support and a fair opportunity to respond, subject to necessary safeguards for the investigation. Decisions must draw on relevant clinical and care expertise. Front-line experience must inform the process alongside safeguarding expertise, and decisions must be open to proper challenge.

You announced today a national oversight arrangement, a national social care intelligence hub and a national safeguarding risk register. These may help improve consistency and identify emerging risks, but they must also demonstrate how they will improve outcomes on the ground for vulnerable people and support timely, effective decision-making in front-line services.

We must also examine the effect on recruitment and retention. If foster families withdraw because of how allegations are handled, the Government must establish why. It must examine what any loss of placements means for that child needing a stable, suitable home. The same scrutiny must apply to concerns about nurses, doctors, social care workers leaving their roles. You must explain how existing arrangements of these proposed reforms will protect vulnerable people, how unnecessary duplication is prevented and who takes responsibility if investigations drift. Before introducing further requirements, identify the gap they address and demonstrate how they will improve safety.

I call for a review of existing arrangements, their effectiveness, proportionality, delays and support for everyone affected. That review must listen to children, families, patients, front-line workers and safeguarding professionals, and publish clear findings and actions. Accountability cannot stop with a nurse on a ward or the foster carer in their home. It must extend to those managing investigations and setting those policies. Our constituents deserve protection. Those caring for them deserve fair treatment. The Government must deliver both. Diolch.

We have to keep learning. We have to keep seeing where there are gaps that need to be filled, where those risks keep evolving. So, this is something that—. I'm really proud that we are setting down this framework, but a framework is only going to exist if all of those components within it keep it erected in the air, afloat, depending on what the metaphor is. But, no, thank you, Claire. Diolch yn fawr iawn.

contributions.text_english:
Thank you, Deputy Minister, for your statement. I definitely concur with you that safeguarding is one of the most important responsibilities of any Government, and I wanted to focus my remarks on children today. You've just said then that you get lessons from the various reviews that are brought forward, and, unfortunately, recent child practice reviews have identified a number of recurring themes, including problems with information sharing, inconsistent application of safeguarding thresholds, and insufficient focus on the child's voice. And therein lies our challenge, doesn't it, really? It's taking policy into practice and making sure that that is implemented in a way that keeps children safe.

It was very good to see you accepting all the recommendations of the Jan Pickles safeguarding review, including on a ministerial safeguarding board. And of course, in 2024, under the previous Government, Wales was the first in the UK to introduce a single unified safeguarding review process, and that included the Wales safeguarding repository. So, I wanted to ask about the commitment in your statement to a national social care intelligence hub and how that would build on the work of the safeguarding repository.

I note as well the commitment to an adult and child protection authority for Wales, and that wasn't recommended in Jan Pickles's review, but it was a recommendation of the independent inquiry into child sexual abuse, and I would certainly support anything that strengthens protections for children and young people. But it would be good to hear you say a little bit about why you've taken that decision to go down that particular road. We're all acutely aware that social care services are stretched financially, and so are those vital services that deal with early intervention with families. So, I'd be keen to hear more about whether you're planning to announce dedicated funding for stronger safeguarding for a safer Wales.

Now, it's been nearly a year since I stood up in the Senedd to make a statement on 'Our Bravery Brought Justice'. That report was the most sobering thing I had ever read since becoming an MS, and parts of it, literally, took my breath away. Now, the overriding failure, really, that ran right the way through that report was the failure to listen to the voice of the child on, literally, countless occasions. Now, you've referred to the importance of children's voice today and embedding that in the work that you're doing, but what I would like to hear is some more detail as to how you are going to do that, because children's voice can't just be an issue for agencies out there—it has to be embedded in the Government's efforts to safeguard children.

Criminal and sexual exploitation of children remains a very serious issue, and one of the problems in this area is the fact that so many vulnerable children, looked-after children, children on the edge of care, are going missing too often. Now, there have been calls for statutory return-home interviews, because, at the moment, there are different practices amongst local authorities and police forces. Can I ask if that is something that you will consider as part of the work that you're doing on children?

And I can see that the Cabinet Minister for education is in the Chamber today, which is good to see. Obviously, it's crucial that there is joint working across Government to protect children. I know that you're still committed to the follow-on work on safeguarding in education, but can I ask how you intend to work with the Cabinet Minister on those issues in education, and particularly on things that we know expose children to more risks, such as exclusion, which can lead to them being more vulnerable to exploitation? Thank you.
