contributions.text_english:
Diolch, Lynne, and I know that this is something that—. You have tremendous expertise in this area and dedication over many years, and I thank you for that. Of course, what we are doing here is building on a lot of work that was done by the previous Government and, again, I'm grateful to you for leading a lot of that work.

And in terms of how the—. I'm grateful that you've welcomed a number of the separate components of what I've been announcing today. You asked specifically a little more about how the central intelligence hub will work in practice. As I've set out, in terms of spotting patterns and gaps and helping to set priorities, a lot of this data or the intelligence already exists, but if we were to ensure that—. That would include things like insights arising from single unified safeguarding reviews. If we can bring those insights together to develop a greater national understanding of where different patterns are and where these risks are emerging, so that—. Because it's, deeply worryingly, something where so many risks evolve and emerge, we need to keep looking to make sure that something doesn't get lost or thought of as, 'Oh, well, that's something that is isolated. That couldn't possibly happen here.' We can never think in that way.

And I suppose this intelligence hub, which would be under the National Office of Care and Support, would be—. We'd want a dedicated safeguarding arm of that to bring all of that intelligence together. It would do things like spotting risks that cross organisational boundaries, that cross geographical boundaries, and make sure that that evidence helps to set priorities nationally, and make sure as well that—. I said earlier that a lot of this information is already available publicly. We are going to be establishing—well, I think we're, certainly, looking at establishing—a number of task-and-finish groups to look at how exactly this data can be used, how we can be guided, and I would welcome any Members with expertise in this area, including you, Lynne, if you have thoughts on how that should evolve, I'd really like to draw on your expertise with that.

You asked particularly about 'Our Bravery Brought Justice' and the voice of the child, which, if there is one thing that is a common theme running throughout this work and this, whether we look at it as a structure, whether we look at it as architecture, the fundamental cornerstone of all of it is making sure that children, when something goes wrong, either their voice is heard if they've raised that concern themselves, or someone is looking out for them and that gets heard and that gets spotted. It is something that—. I'm really determined that we have to make sure that this system is informed by those voices.

If we look at 'Our Bravery Brought Justice', the name of that report says it all. Children should never have had to have been that brave in the first place. We have to make sure that something like that doesn't happen again. We have to take every action possible to try to make sure that that doesn't happen again. And again, very often, we need to make sure that the services we have—. Even if they're well-meaning, they're not always trauma-informed, they're not always person-centred. We need to make sure that this is something that, again, as you have alluded to, is cross-Government. It's something that I'll be working really closely with the Cabinet Minister for education on, certainly, but across health, across social care, across so many different aspects, this is something that will come into so many elements of children's and young people's and adults' lives. Phase 2 of the review is looking at sport, at faith, at religious groups. We need to be looking across different sectors.

You asked about statutory return-home interviews, and, yes, that is something that is definitely under consideration. I think it is £700,000 that has been set aside for the work on safeguarding, but there is other work from other budget expenditure lines that is coming together, because, of course, this is, again, a cross-Government initiative.

But I would say, again, that there are Members across this Chamber who have had disclosures made to them, who have had horrendous experiences themselves or have known people who have gone through terrible things, and you will know more than anyone that we owe it to people who have gone through something terrible to get it right for people in the future. Their voices have to shape those improvements. So, diolch, Lynne, for those questions.

contributions.text_english:
Thank you, Deputy Minister, for this afternoon's statement. Putting stronger safeguards in place is something to be welcomed, but it must be more than just about structures, strategies and warm words from the Welsh Government. It is about whether a child or vulnerable adult at risk is identified early, whether concerns are acted upon and whether there is a joined-up approach from agencies working at pace to help keep people safe.

We must also learn from the past. I don't intend to go over the specific details today, as I am sure we are all aware of the situation, but we must learn from incidents such as the Neil Foden case. Following Foden's imprisonment for 17 years after being convicted of 19 sexual abuse offences, a child practice review was indeed held. That review found that there were more than 50 missed opportunities to intervene and stop the predator headteacher from sexually abusing children. The failings we saw in this were utterly sickening, and we must agree that it never—and I mean never—is allowed to be repeated ever again. So, how will the Welsh Government ensure that cases like these are taken into account as part of this piece of work?

In April 2025, the Supreme Court ruled that sex is defined as biological sex only—a welcome decision for women and girls across Wales. However, since then, we have seen dither and delay from the Welsh Government and other public bodies in ensuring that this ruling is adhered to, especially when it comes to single-sex spaces. So, Deputy Minister, do you agree with me that ensuring that the judgment is adhered to and implemented consistently across Wales is an important part of improving safeguarding?

Deputy Minister, whilst I welcome the Government's aim of delivering stronger safeguarding for a safer Wales, there are some important questions about how this is actually going to work. You say that the Government will strengthen national leadership, oversight and accountability, but who will ultimately be accountable if safeguarding arrangements fail, and what consequences will there be when agencies do not perform effectively? Deputy Minister, I am curious to know what, if anything, these proposed reforms will mean for staff on the front line, like social workers and teachers. What specific improvements will they see as a result of this piece of work?

Sticking with those on the front line, another obvious question is about whether the system has sufficient capacity. We know that there are severe staff shortages across the board, so is the workforce there to successfully bring these changes forward? If not, where will the extra capacity needed be coming from?

Also, Deputy Minister, what are the financial implications of these reforms? In your statement, you outlined plans to create a national social care intelligence hub, a national safeguarding plan and a national safeguarding risk register. When do you expect all of these to be operational? I'd really like to have some dates in place.

A joined-up approach between the various agencies is going to be instrumental in improving safeguards. That means better data sharing, which is something we all know previous Welsh Governments have seriously lacked on over the years. So, how will these reforms provide this joined-up approach when it comes to data sharing between sectors like health, education, social care and policing? I welcome the Government's commitment to ensuring consistency and protection across all parts of Wales. Nobody—and I mean nobody—should be at a disadvantage just because of their postcode. So, how is the Government going to measure whether these safeguards are applied consistently across the country?

Deputy Minister, talking about lived experience, it will be vital in relation to this going forward, and the voices of children and adults should be heard and should be at the heart of these reforms. So, can I please get a commitment from you that it will be the case and, if so, can you elaborate on how exactly they're going to be feeding into this? Deputy Minister, the proof will ultimately be in the pudding. The $1 million question is whether these reforms will make people feel safe in the long term, and I sincerely hope that they do, but what specific outcomes does the Government expect to improve and by when? Thank you.

contributions.text_english:
Diolch, Natasha, for those questions. As you've said, this has to be about making improvements to people's lives. This can't just be about what's down on a piece of paper, it can't just be what is collected in graphs. It's about whether what is collected is analysed effectively, whether it leads to action and whether that action translates into saving and improving people's lives, because that's the stuff that we're really talking about here. So, none of us will lose sight of that, of course. You've alluded to cases in the past where too many missed opportunities have been missed opportunities to act. We have to learn from those. We have to do everything in our power to save children and adults at risk in the future.

And, yes, this Government has committed to adhering to the law—always, of course. And we have also committed always to protecting those groups and those people who are at greatest risk and who are vulnerable in our society, and there are many facets to this. That is something that the Deputy First Minister has always been consistent on.

In terms of what you asked about what this will mean for front-line staff, well, this, of course, will mean empowering front-line staff. Because there will be so many missed opportunities that staff themselves will have flagged, when different staff might have spotted something, whether that was in one area or the same patterns emerging in different places. This will mean that we are ensuring that those staff voices will be amplified and that they won't be standing in isolation any more.

And, of course, as I mentioned to Claire, we're going to have to look at training and making sure that staff, in order to be empowered, are able to use the—. To make sure that they are aware of how this is going to change their work, but it is about empowering them and not putting further burdens on them. Because, of course, a lot of this, in terms of—. You asked about capacity. This is workable because an awful lot of this is not creating new obligations; this is about when staff are spotting things, when staff are doing their jobs, that we are gaining that national picture and that we have greater cohesiveness across the piece. So, it isn't about creating new forms or anything like that that staff will need to fill in; it's about making sure that every contact counts and that every voice is listened to.

You asked some specific questions about when, and I mentioned earlier that this is going to be a phased programme of work, so that where there are things we can do immediately, we can act very quickly on those at the same time as progressing some of the work that, as I've mentioned, is going to take further time and further consultation in some of these areas as well. In terms of the ministerial oversight board, the plan is to establish that certainly by the beginning of next year.

In terms of the national safeguarding plan and the national risk register, the time frame—. So, I think that we are determining at the moment whether it will cover three years or five years, but there will be annual deliverables and it's something that we are going to be working on over the next two years to establish, in terms of making sure that we know what a good system looks like. Again, that is with the hope of consulting on an adult and child protection authority in the future. So, again, this is phased because we don't want to do something that is then going to—. Diolch, Deputy Llywydd. To declare an interest, I've got a close family member working in the NHS.

Deputy Minister, nobody disputes the importance of safeguarding. No-one disputes that children need to be safe from neglect, harm or abuse, and in that way, the statement's right. But we have to be realistic about what is happening on the ground in Wales. Across Wales, we have more than 7,000 looked-after children, around 4,800 living in foster placement, yet Wales needs 550 new foster carers every year. And at a time when the numbers of foster carers are declining, demands continue to rise. In Wales, more than 20 per cent of foster parents who left cited safeguarding allegations as the reason.

We also hear of too many cases of individuals in fostering, education, care and other professions spending months or years under safeguarding investigations. They can't move on with their lives, despite no wrongdoing ever being proven. Doctors face triple jeopardy: investigated by the police, the General Medical Council and the trust all at the same time as trying to work, if they're not off with stress. Nearly one in three who experience fitness-to-practice investigations experience suicidal thoughts, and sometimes investigations go on for years.

Does the Minister accept that safeguarding systems must protect the vulnerable, but must also be proportionate, timely and fair to those who are accused? As you say in the statement, we owe it to them to get this right.

The motion calls on the Welsh and UK Governments to work together in three key areas: enhancing Wales's fiscal flexibilities, to review the operation of the Barnett formula and to reaffirm support for the UK Government's commitment to invest £14 billion in rail infrastructure across Wales. These are practical, achievable steps that can help to strengthen our economy, support public services and improve people's lives. They are not asks for special treatment. They are asks for a collaborative approach to lead to better outcomes for Wales.

Fiscal flexibilities, therefore. The First Minister has been clear that the Welsh Government faces an exceptionally challenging financial outlook, with next year's budget expected to be lower in real terms than this year's. While demands on our public services, our infrastructure and economy continue to grow, the funding available to us is not keeping pace. Current forecasts point to a real-terms reduction in our resource budget of 0.7 per cent in 2027-28, while our capital budget is expected to be around 9 per cent lower in real terms by the end of the spending review period in 2030.

That challenge may become even greater once the implications of recent announcements by the UK Government on defence spending become clearer. In these circumstances, it's more important than ever that Wales has fair funding and the fiscal powers and flexibility needed to meet emerging challenges, invest in our priorities and deliver for communities across Wales. Ensuring that Wales has the tools to manage its own finances effectively is essential if decisions about Wales are to reflect Wales's needs and priorities.

In-year announcements from the UK Government, changing spending profiles and unforeseen economic circumstances can all have substantial impacts on our budget planning. But under current arrangements, the Welsh Government only has limited access to its own reserve and more restricted fiscal flexibilities than other parts of the UK. The Welsh Government has had to seek temporary waivers to Wales reserve restrictions in three of the last four years. That is not an effective way to manage public finances. We should not have to ask the UK Government each year for flexibilities that are already available elsewhere in the UK. I'm therefore seeking to place these temporary arrangements, which we have had to rely on repeatedly, on a permanent footing, providing greater certainty and supporting effective budget planning.

Removing restrictions on the Wales reserve is a practical first step. It would allow Wales to make better use of resources that already belong to Wales and bring our arrangements closer to those available in Scotland. Without full access to the Wales reserve, I will only be able to draw down £200 million, which is well under 1 per cent of the Wales budget, to assist with known and emerging pressures. This includes the impacts of funding announcements by the UK Government in year, such as the expected cuts in our capital settlement because of increased defence spending.

Of course, these issues extend beyond the operation of the Wales reserve alone. The case for greater flexibility highlights a broader question about whether Wales's fiscal arrangements remain fit for purpose. That's why I have proposed a review of the Wales fiscal framework. A decade has passed since the fiscal framework was agreed in 2016. Wales has changed. The economic environment has changed. The constitutional landscape has changed. It's reasonable to ask whether the current arrangements remain fit for purpose and whether they provide Wales with the resilience and flexibility required to meet future challenges.

As part of that review, I will be looking to address a variety of issues, including the operation and flexibility of the Wales reserve and the adequacy of Wales's borrowing powers—and remember that local authorities have greater flexibilities than the Welsh Government has. We also need to look at the effectiveness of current funding arrangements in reflecting relative need and the case for further tax devolution. The Welsh Government plans to seek further income tax devolution and the devolution of air passenger duty. We will also be separately seeking competence for a new vacant land tax.

These issues go beyond the motion before the Senedd today, but I can also give you this commitment today: I will not agree, as finance Minister, a revised fiscal framework unless it is a good deal for Wales, and the opinion of the Senedd on this will be an important consideration as the review proceeds.

Mae'r cynnig yn galw ar Lywodraethau Cymru a'r Deyrnas Gyfunol i weithio gyda'n gilydd mewn tri maes allweddol: i wella hyblygrwydd cyllidol Cymru, i adolygu gweithrediad fformiwla Barnett ac i ailddatgan cefnogaeth i ymrwymiad Llywodraeth y Deyrnas Gyfunol i fuddsoddi £14 biliwn mewn seilwaith rheilffyrdd ledled Cymru. Mae'r rhain yn gamau ymarferol, cyraeddadwy a all helpu i gryfhau ein heconomi, cefnogi gwasanaethau cyhoeddus a gwella bywydau pobl. Nid ydynt yn geisiadau am driniaeth arbennig. Maent yn geisiadau am ddull cydweithredol a fydd yn arwain at ganlyniadau gwell i Gymru.

Hyblygrwydd cyllidol, felly. Mae'r Prif Weinidog wedi bod yn glir bod Llywodraeth Cymru yn wynebu rhagolygon ariannol eithriadol o heriol, gyda disgwyl i gyllideb y flwyddyn nesaf fod yn is mewn termau real nag eleni. Tra bo'r galw ar ein gwasanaethau cyhoeddus, ein seilwaith a'n heconomi yn parhau i gynyddu, nid yw'r cyllid sydd ar gael inni yn cadw cam â hyn. Mae'r rhagolygon cyfredol yn dangos gostyngiad termau real yn ein cyllideb adnodd o 0.7 y cant yn ystod 2027-28, tra bod disgwyl i'r gyllideb gyfalaf fod tua 9 y cant yn is mewn termau real erbyn diwedd cyfnod yr adolygiad gwariant yn 2030.

Gallai'r her hon ddod yn fwy fyth unwaith y bydd goblygiadau cyhoeddiadau diweddar Llywodraeth y Deyrnas Gyfunol ar wariant amddiffyn yn gliriach i ni. Yn yr amgylchiadau hyn, mae'n bwysicach nag erioed bod gan Gymru gyllid teg, y pwerau cyllidol a'r hyblygrwydd sydd eu hangen i gwrdd â heriau, buddsoddi yn ein blaenoriaethau a chyflawni ar gyfer cymunedau. Mae sicrhau bod gan Gymru'r offer i reoli ei chyllid ei hun yn effeithiol yn hanfodol er mwyn i benderfyniadau am Gymru adlewyrchu anghenion a blaenoriaethau Cymru. 

Gall cyhoeddiadau yn ystod y flwyddyn gan Lywodraeth y Deyrnas Gyfunol, newidiadau i broffiliau gwariant ac amgylchiadau economaidd annisgwyl oll gael effaith sylweddol ar ein gwaith o gynllunio'r gyllideb. Ond o dan y trefniadau presennol, dim ond mynediad cyfyngedig i'n cronfa wrth gefn sydd gan Lywodraeth Cymru a hyblygrwydd cyllidol mwy cyfyngedig na rhannau eraill o'r Deyrnas Gyfunol. Bu'n rhaid i Lywodraeth Cymru ofyn am hepgoriadau dros dro i gyfyngiadau'r cronfa wrth gefn mewn tair o'r pedair blynedd ddiwethaf. Nid yw hynny'n ffordd effeithiol o reoli cyllid cyhoeddus. Ni ddylem orfod gofyn i Lywodraeth y Deyrnas Gyfunol bob blwyddyn am yr hyblygrwydd sydd eisoes ar gael mewn rhannau eraill o'r Deyrnas Unedig. Felly, rwy'n ceisio rhoi'r trefniadau dros dro hyn, y bu'n rhaid dibynnu arnynt dro ar ôl tro, ar sail barhaol, gan ddarparu mwy o sicrwydd a chefnogi gwaith effeithiol o gynllunio'r gyllideb.

Mae dileu'r cyfyngiadau ar gronfa wrth gefn Cymru yn gam cyntaf ymarferol. Byddai hynny'n caniatáu i Gymru wneud gwell defnydd o adnoddau sydd eisoes yn perthyn i Gymru ac yn dod â'n trefniadau yn nes at y rhai sydd ar gael yn yr Alban. Heb fynediad llawn at gronfa wrth gefn, dim ond £200 miliwn y byddaf i'n gallu ei thynnu i lawr, sef ymhell o dan 1 y cant o gyllideb Cymru, er mwyn helpu i ymdrin â phwysau y gwyddom amdanynt eisoes a phwysau sy'n dod i'r amlwg. Mae hyn yn cynnwys effeithiau cyhoeddiadau ariannu Llywodraeth y Deyrnas Gyfunol o fewn blwyddyn, megis y toriadau disgwyliedig i'n setliad cyfalaf o ganlyniad i gynnydd mewn gwariant ar amddiffyn.

Wrth gwrs, mae'r materion yn ymestyn y tu hwnt i weithrediad cronfa wrth gefn Cymru yn unig. Mae'r achos dros fwy o hyblygrwydd yn tynnu sylw at gwestiwn ehangach ynghylch a yw trefniadau cyllidol Cymru yn parhau i fod yn addas. Dyna pam yr wyf yn cynnig adolygiad o fframwaith cyllidol Cymru. Mae degawd wedi mynd heibio ers i'r fframwaith cyllidol gael ei gytuno yn 2016. Mae Cymru wedi newid. Mae'r amgylchedd economaidd wedi newid. Mae'r dirwedd gyfansoddiadol wedi newid. Mae'n rhesymol gofyn a yw'r trefniadau presennol yn parhau i fod yn addas i'r diben ac a ydynt yn rhoi'r gwytnwch a'r hyblygrwydd sydd eu hangen i Gymru i gwrdd â heriau yn y dyfodol. 

Fel rhan o'r adolygiad, byddaf eisiau mynd i'r afael ag amrywiaeth o faterion, gan gynnwys gweithrediad a hyblygrwydd cronfa wrth gefn Cymru a digonolrwydd pwerau benthyca Cymru—a chofiwch fod gan awdurdodau lleol fwy o hyblygrwydd cyllidol nag sydd gan Lywodraeth Cymru. Hefyd mae angen edrych ar effeithiolrwydd y trefniadau cyllido presennol o ran adlewyrchu angen cymharol a'r achos dros ddatganoli treth pellach. Mae Llywodraeth Cymru yn bwriadu ceisio datganoli pwerau pellach dros dreth incwm, ynghyd â datganoli'r doll teithwyr awyr. Byddwn hefyd yn ceisio cymhwysedd deddfwriaethol ar wahân ar gyfer treth newydd ar dir gwag.

Mae'r materion hyn yn mynd y tu hwnt i'r cynnig sydd gerbron y Senedd heddiw, ond gallaf roi'r ymrwymiad hwn ichi heddiw: ni fyddaf yn cytuno, fel Gweinidog cyllid, i fframwaith cyllidol diwygiedig oni bai ei fod yn gynnig da i Gymru, a bydd barn y Senedd yma ar hynny yn ystyriaeth bwysig wrth i’r adolygiad fynd yn ei flaen.

I want to be clear: recent UK Government funding settlements have provided additional resources for Wales, and we recognise that. Next year’s settlement, however, is negative in real terms. However, any increased funding does not automatically mean fair funding, nor does it necessarily provide sufficient resources to meet growing demands or address where there has been historical underinvestment by the UK Government.

The pressures facing public services remain significant. The NHS continues to face increasing demand, local authorities and other public services continue to face substantial financial pressures, while persistent inflation continues to erode the real-terms value of public spending. These pressures reinforce the need to consider whether current funding arrangements adequately reflect Wales's needs.

My priority is to improve the operation of the Barnett formula while also exploring, over the medium term, whether a more needs-based approach could better support communities across Wales. All systems can be improved. I do not underestimate the challenge. The Treasury's instinct will often be to resist changes to established funding arrangements or the transfer of additional fiscal powers. However, we must move beyond viewing these issues as a zero-sum game, and we must believe that the spirit of the new Prime Minister to support more devolution from Whitehall will reach even the darkest corners of the UK Treasury in the coming weeks and months.

I also realise that there will be a variety of views across this Chamber on the need for reforming or replacing the Barnett formula. In the interest of building consensus, that is why this motion concentrates only on its operation. This is about ensuring that the system commands confidence, operates transparently and enables funding decisions to be clearly understood by governments and citizens alike.

As an illustration, we have limited visibility over how comparability percentages are determined and how changes at fiscal events are assessed by the Treasury. These decisions directly affect our funding. There should be a structured and timely process through which we can challenge or seek clarification.

We have already secured an action through the Finance: Interministerial Standing Committee to make practical improvements to the operation of the Barnett formula, increase transparency around funding decisions and remove constraints that limit our ability to invest in and improve Welsh public services. This work was started in the interministerial group by my predecessor, and new Ministers in our meeting in September agreed that this work must deliver tangible progress before we meet again in the new year. 

Finally for this opening introduction, Llywydd, the third part of the motion. For decades, Wales has experienced significant underinvestment in rail infrastructure. That is why we welcomed the UK Government's recommitment to invest £14 billion in Welsh rail infrastructure through the joint UK-Wales rail board vision, ‘Today, Tomorrow, Together’. I would also like to acknowledge the amount of work undertaken by the previous Welsh Government in its development.

However, commitments alone do not improve connectivity. What matters now is delivery. At present, only £302 million has been allocated for the enhancement of non-devolved rail infrastructure in Wales during the current spending review period. That represents little more than 1 per cent of Network Rail spending in England and Wales over the same period.

The consequences of this long-term underinvestment extend beyond the rail network itself. Insufficient rail capacity and connectivity have limited travel choices for many communities, contributing to greater reliance on road transport, increased congestion on key routes such as the M4, as we heard earlier this afternoon, and higher transport-related emissions. Strengthening rail infrastructure is, therefore, not simply about improving train services; it is about creating a more resilient, sustainable and integrated transport network for Wales as a whole.

Delivering the £14 billion commitment is an important step towards addressing decades of underinvestment in Wales's rail infrastructure and the legitimate concerns felt across Wales that we did not benefit from HS2 consequentials, despite the scale of rail investment elsewhere in the UK. Not receiving a consequential for HS2 has meant that we have not been able to choose to use that additional funding that would have come into our budget to invest in our own priorities for rail, roads or wider transport infrastructure.

We now need agreement on a delivery programme and a clear timeline for the £14 billion rail investment commitment. The UK Government must substantially increase current levels of investment to deliver the Burns and other stations, including in north Wales, that were committed to at the UK spending review in 2025. Doing so would improve connectivity, support economic growth and enable the development of future projects for the next spending review period, while beginning to address the historic underfunding of rail in Wales. We therefore want to see an additional £1 billion of the £14 billion commitment invested during the current spending review period, up to 2029-30. 

Better connectivity links people to jobs, businesses to markets and communities to opportunities. Every part of Wales deserves the benefits that modern transport infrastructure can bring. If we can build consensus on what Wales needs, we'll be in a stronger position to secure the investment, powers and funding arrangements necessary to ensure that Wales's interests and needs are fully reflected in the UK autumn budget and future UK Government decisions.

I look forward, this afternoon, to hearing the views of Members across the Chamber. I hope that there will be clarity on what unites us on fiscal reform. We will always be stronger in making our case for Wales when we speak with one voice. Diolch yn fawr.

contributions.text_english:
Before I get into the meat of this debate, I have to ask: what really is the point of tabling this motion today and taking up an hour of Welsh taxpayers' time? The motion was co-tabled by the Plaid Cymru Government and its little helpers, in a spectacular reversal of roles, Welsh Labour. So, unless there is some kind of revolt going to happen on the back benches, we already know what the outcome will be. And yet here we are, spending a full hour of our lives on it, when we could be doing something useful for our constituents.

This Chamber has already come under fire recently for how it spends its time. I saw a post on X, viewed more than 300,000 times, showing last week's Plenary and the row over the word 'blanket'. The caption of the post read:

'Oh my god. This isn't a sketch. This is real. It happened at the Welsh Senedd. Madness'.

We as a Parliament have to be very careful that we are spending our time here wisely, that we are addressing the challenges that the Welsh public is facing, that we walk in their shoes, that we get it. I'm afraid I do not think that the public would put fiscal reform anywhere near the top of their agenda.

Now to the contents of the motion itself. In it, the Welsh Government is asking the Senedd to call on the Welsh Government to work with the UK Government. You already do that, don't you? Working with the UK Government is a fundamental part of a devolved Government's responsibilities. Welsh Labour did it for 27 years when they were in power and your own Government has been doing it ever since. You do not need the Senedd to hold your hand while you speak to Andy Burnham.

My other issue on this motion is the utter vagueness of the wording. Part (a) states:

'enhance the Welsh Government’s fiscal flexibilities'.

Which ones and to what extent? You say that that includes

'removal of all restrictions on the Wales Reserve'.

But, of course, you're asking for much more than that. So, why not be honest and write exactly what it is you are calling for?

Reform's position is clear and unequivocal: prioritise doing better with the existing powers. Deliver better results with the money you have. The Welsh Government and civil service need to prove that they can deliver first-class public services efficiently. Reform welcomes your clear commitment to more transparency, as outlined by the Cabinet Minister for Government effectiveness, but so far, year after year, all we see is more economic decline and an NHS in Wales that is sinking financially.

On part (b),

'review the operation of the Barnett Formula to strengthen fairness and transparency',

I understand that your argument at first is about transparency and reporting, but this is politics. The wording is so general and so open to interpretation that if this motion is agreed, we may well hear a Plaid Government, down the line, suggest that the Senedd backed fundamental change to the Barnett formula and demand more funding on the back of it.

Specifics matter. Precise wording matters. If the Welsh Government knows which fiscal powers it wants, it should name them, cost them and explain the safeguards. If it cannot do that, then this motion is not a plan for reform, it is a request for political cover for the lack of ideas on the left.

I hope the theme of this speech was clear: please, for the sake of the people of Wales, say in clear words what exactly you're asking for, and please remember that our time belongs to the people of Wales and they expect us to use it wisely. Diolch, Lywydd.

Well, I'll try and use my time wisely, then, and I look forward to having no more contributions from the Reform benches as we get straight to the vote. [Laughter.]

Let me be clear, Welsh Labour is proud to co-table this motion, welcoming and reaffirming support for the UK Labour Government's transformative £14 billion commitment for Welsh rail infrastructure. I'm delighted, a bit cheeky, that our co-tablers feel able to welcome this commitment rather than their previous position, which was to question the seriousness with which both Labour Governments at the time were determined to boost rail infrastructure in Wales. Look, we all recognise the underfunding that has resulted off the back of HS2. That £14 billion makes that good and then some. I'm pleased that Members from across the Senedd will also have the chance to put on record their support for this generational commitment. I'll take Cai's as read, right?

We all know how important public transport is to improve people's quality of life, to create jobs, to link communities and to bring people closer together, and to encourage economic growth and prosperity. We heard that in the debate on the Menai crossing and the M4. But, for too long, our rail infrastructure has been prevented from reaching its potential by successive Conservative Governments in Westminster that failed to invest in Wales. That changed in 2024 when a Labour Government was elected in the UK, meaning that Wales had two Labour Governments at the time that could work together. And through that collaboration, the two Governments managed to commit to historic levels of investment in Welsh rail infrastructure and to double the long-term plan for Welsh rail, bringing a welcome end to the 14 years of neglect and underspend.

The investment will transform communities across Wales, including the five Burns station between Cardiff and the Severn Tunnel Junction, and improve capacity and accessibility in Cardiff Central station, which is the busiest station in Wales, and also start the north Wales network by improving rail crossings and undertaking that crucial work to get more regular services. The project will also help to build a pipeline for planning the next generation of improvements across Wales.

A pipeline of potentially 43 projects, 12,000 jobs in every part of Wales, with some examples including new stations in Swansea and west Wales, including at St Clears, improved services to Milford Haven, Pembroke Dock and Fishguard, direct services to Liverpool, the Wirral and Wrexham, and stronger links to Deeside industrial park, as well as plans to upgrade the north Wales main line and more reliable trains and services on the Cambrian line. These generational commitments will help deliver the transport network that Wales deserves and show the benefit of having a UK Labour Government that is committed to investing in Wales. I know from Ministers in Westminster that the UK Labour Government is working to deliver these plans as quickly as possible, and I can give my assurance that the benches here will work with the Government here in Wales to secure those commitments.

On the issue of fair funding, as the party of devolution, Welsh Labour is also proud to reiterate our long-standing calls for the Barnett formula to be reviewed and for the Welsh Government's fiscal flexibilities to be enhanced. Welsh Labour has always pushed for more funding and more powers for Wales as part of a strong United Kingdom.

contributions.text_english:
Thanks to the two Labour Governments working together, we managed to secure additional powers in this area, including in relation to the expenditure of reserves. We are clear that those changes should continue and be permanent. But, as has been an issue for a series of Welsh Governments over the years, it's also appropriate that Wales gets its fair share of funding. That does mean reform of the Barnett formula. In our manifesto this year, Welsh Labour made the case for a new 'fair share formula', which would ensure that Wales receives its proper share of UK resources automatically in all-important areas.

We also worked to ensure the reform of Barnett to create a system that is based on need and works for all parts of the UK. We recognise that the only way, ultimately, of reaching a system that is based on need is through negotiation and securing agreement between the four nations of the United Kingdom, and, in that regard, I would question how productive it is to for the Welsh First Minister to be grandstanding on this issue by placing the whole responsibility for fairer funding entirely on the shoulders of the UK Prime Minister, as he did over the weekend.

We know that the Scottish Government continues to evade demands for a system based on need, so I think the Welsh Government has a key role in making the case to secure an agreement across the nations of the UK. I'm running out of time.

Dŷn ni'n glir y dylai'r newidiadau hynny barhau yn barhaol. Yn ein maniffesto ni eleni, gwnaeth Llafur Cymru gyflwyno'r achos dros 'fformiwla cyfran deg' newydd a fyddai wedi sicrhau bod Cymru'n derbyn ei chyfran o adnoddau'r Deyrnas Gyfunol yn awtomatig mewn meysydd hollbwysig.

Mi wnaethon ni hefyd ymrwymo i weithio i sicrhau diwygio Barnett er mwyn creu system sy'n seiliedig ar angen ac sy'n gweithio i bob rhan o'r Deyrnas Gyfunol. Rydym ni'n cydnabod mai'r unig ffordd yn y pen draw o gyrraedd system sy'n seiliedig ar angen yw drwy drafod a sicrhau cytundeb rhwng y pedair cenedl yn y Deyrnas Gyfunol, ac, yn hynny o beth, byddwn i'n cwestiynu pa mor gynhyrchiol yw hi i Brif Weinidog Cymru 'grandstand-io' ar y mater hwn drwy roi'r cyfrifoldeb cyfan am gyllid tecach yn unig ar ysgwyddau Prif Weinidog y Deyrnas Gyfunol, fel roedd e'n gwneud dros y penwythnos.

I'll begin by stating the obvious: the case for Wales's fiscal reform is, as far as Plaid Cymru is concerned, cut and dried. Independent commissions and expert reports have repeatedly identified the limitations of the current arrangements. Most recently, the Independent Commission on the Constitutional Future of Wales set out a clear case for greater fiscal autonomy, and now with Plaid Cymru in Government, we have an opportunity to take that clear-eyed analysis and turn it into a programme of practical reform. Because, ultimately, the question we should ask of our fiscal framework is a very straightforward one: does it give Wales the flexibility we need to sufficiently deal with the scale of the challenges we face?

The fiscal framework established limits on both the size of the Wales reserve, £385 million, and annual draw-downs with limits of £137.5 million for revenue and £55 million for capital. This is, of course, in contrast to the Scottish fiscal framework, within which the Scottish Government can draw down as much as they need to. There is simply no justification or compelling reasoning for Wales being treated any differently—none whatsoever. And while it's welcome that the overall limit on the size of the reserve and the annual limit for drawing down both capital and revenue spending has increased by 10 per cent, it still falls woefully short and does nothing to restore the large inflationary losses to these limits since they were set in cash terms a decade ago. This is not bloodless constitutional abstraction. It has implications for our ability to build up and use resources for future investment, whether that be in infrastructure, public services or the economy. And where there is insufficient capacity within the reserve, the ceiling for putting money in is set at 1.4 per cent of our budget. The Treasury can simply claw that money back.

The same absurdities apply to our borrowing powers, and whilst not included in this motion, Llywydd, I'm going to mention it anyway. Less expensive forms of borrowing are subject to strict limits: £1.1 billion, with an annual limit of £165 million via the national loan fund. If the Welsh Government wishes to undertake a project above a certain scale, it must either take this money from public services, borrow it privately via the mutual investment model, or hope that the UK Government decides to undertake a project of a similar scale in England and that it delivers on Barnett consequentials.

The Welsh Government has responsibility for huge areas of policy. The very principle of devolution is predicated on the notion that the people of Wales should be able to elect a Government that can pursue different priorities and make different choices from Governments elsewhere in the UK. But meaningful political responsibility requires meaningful fiscal powers, and we currently operate within a system that actively inhibits our ability to raise, save and borrow the resources necessary to deliver on the vast range of devolved responsibilities.

I'm conscious that the word 'limit' is one that I've used a lot during this contribution, but it's an apt characterisation of our fiscal framework: it is both limited and limiting. The current system of occasional ad hoc flexibilities afforded to the Welsh Government at the Treasury's discretion militates against our democracy. This is not a sustainable basis on which to take our ambitions for Wales forward. The restrictions on the Welsh Government's access to the reserve should be removed permanently, bringing Wales in line with Scotland. The current limits are debilitating and the fiscal framework needs to be reformed.

contributions.text_english:
Well, here we go again: Labour and Plaid Cymru lecturing this Senedd on fiscal reform, which, to many of my constituents, will be somewhat like Bonnie and Clyde asking to look after the bank over lunch time. Whilst you admire the confidence, I wouldn't give them the keys. Plaid Cymru and Labour may sit on different sides of this Chamber, but when it comes to the fundamental approach of taxing and spending, we have seen remarkably little appetite for genuine fiscal reform.

Indeed, this current 2026-27 budget was secured through an agreement between Labour and Plaid Cymru, and when Plaid extended to Government, it chose to honour the spending commitments in that budget. So, this debate should not simply be about who spends the money. It should be about something much more fundamental: how Government raises it, how it spends it, whether taxpayers receive value for it, and whether Government itself is prepared to reform, because fiscal reform cannot simply mean changing the name above the door whilst maintaining the same approach underneath it. That is why fiscal reform is ultimately about a choice: a choice between a Government that believes the answer to almost every problem is more spending and more bureaucracy, where Reform UK believes taxpayers have a right to demand value and accountability and results, because Government has no money of its own. [Interruption.] No, thank you.

Every pound spent in this place ultimately comes from taxpayers or borrowing that taxpayers will eventually have to service, and Reform UK starts from a very simple principle: it is taxpayers' money before it is Government's money. That is where I believe the fundamental difference between Reform and Plaid Cymru lies. Plaid Cymru came into Government promising change. Then came its first financial test, the supplementary budget. And what happened? It failed. On 14 July, Plaid Cymru's first supplementary budget was rejected by this Senedd by 49 to 44 votes. Now, Plaid will undoubtedly blame opposition parties, but Government is about more than announcing how much money you want to spend. Government is about leadership. It is all about building confidence in your priorities, demonstrating value for money, and convincing Parliament your financial plans deserve its support. That is precisely why fiscal reform matters, and Plaid cannot pretend that they have nothing to do with the financial settlement that they inherited. Only months earlier, Plaid Cymru negotiated a budget agreement with the previous Labour Government and then abstained to allow the budget to pass. They did not endorse every line of it, but they helped provide the parliamentary route for that financial settlement to take effect.

So, Reform's message on fiscal reform is different. Fiscal reform cannot simply mean spending more, taxing more, creating another scheme. This isn't reform; it's more bureaucracy. Genuine fiscal reforms mean asking the harder questions. What can Government stop doing? What can Government do better? Where is taxpayers' money going and being wasted? And what bureaucracy can be removed? That is what fiscal reform should be about: prioritising expenditure, eliminating waste and ensuring that Government lives within the resources available to it. It commits us to cutting 1p from every £1 across all rates of Welsh income tax by the end of this Senedd term, funded through reductions in expenditure elsewhere without cuts to front-line services, putting more of people's own money back in their pockets. We will review the quango state, merging or abolishing bodies whose functions are duplicated or unnecessary. And we will introduce a tax lock. Reform will not introduce a new Welsh-controlled tax or levy that has not been set out in our manifesto and approved by voters.

That is fiscal reform—lower taxation where it can be afforded, disciplined spending, less waste, and protecting the front-line services upon which people depend, because economic growth does not come from Government's endless moving of taxpayers' money around Cardiff Bay. Prosperity comes from people building businesses, entrepreneurs taking risks, companies investing, and people earning and spending their own money. And Government should create the conditions that allow them to do it. That is the Reform alternative—lower taxes, less waste, less bureaucracy, better infrastructure, stronger front-line services, and a Government that understands that economic growth ultimately pays for public services upon which we all depend.

So, when Plaid Cymru return to this Chamber with further spending plans, Reform should ask a very different question: not simply, 'How much are you spending, and where can savings be redirected towards front-line services in—?' Sorry, bear with me. Apologies. So, this includes politically fashionable projects that Governments are often reluctant to challenge, because fiscal reform requires us to confront spending driven more by ideology than outcomes. The test should not be whether a policy makes a Minister feel virtuous. The test should be: does it work, does it improve people's lives, and is it worth what taxpayers are being charged for it? If the answer is 'no', then Reform should have absolutely no hesitation in challenging that expenditure. There should be no sacred cows here when it comes to taxpayers' money.

Diolch, Lywydd. I'm grateful to be able to take part in this debate this evening. And I must say, Llywydd, it has been far more interesting than I expected when I saw the title of the debate in the first place. I will first of all remind the Labour spokesperson, who seemed to forget about the hundreds of millions of pounds the Conservative Government supported his own city growth region in, especially when it came to the south Wales metro as well. He seems to have completely forgotten about that rail investment over the last Conservative Government here.

We've heard, so far, from Reform, Llywydd—the first speaker who seemed to think that this debate was a complete waste of time, and the second speaker who used nearly six minutes of that time to talk about the importance of fiscal reform and why it matters so much.

I think, Llywydd, it is fair to say that a Government should be in a position to be able to have the right amount of flexibility to respond to pressures that are facing communities across the area that it represents and is responsible for. And I think, as Welsh Conservatives, we want to ensure there's a system in place that gives the appropriate Governments the appropriate amount of flexibility to deal with those issues. And I think, to be fair, the current arrangements are probably unusual, to say the least, in particular around the issue of reserves, Llywydd. I think there's a different argument around borrowing powers, and I think Members will certainly understand the fact that your borrowing power is often related to your ability to raise taxes. That's why local authorities are able to borrow more readily than the Welsh Government, currently. But I think the current arrangements around the Wales reserve is unusual, to say the least, and that's why, as Welsh Conservatives, we would support greater flexibility, in particular around the restrictions that currently exist on the Wales reserve.

And that greater flexibility, though, should also come with making sure there's very clear accountability and scrutiny, because if those restrictions are removed, taxpayers should be able to see how that flexibility is being used and what it is delivering. I think it is reasonable to say that a Government should be able to plan beyond a very small time frame and with very limited flexibility around reserves, in particular.

As I say, the issues around borrowing—I think it's a completely different discussion and argument. Perhaps another one we should have on another day in this Chamber, because I expect the views may be different across this Chamber if that was debated as a single issue.

In relation to the second part of the motion today, which is the review of the operation of the Barnett formula, we would support a review of the operation of the Barnett formula. We believe the current formula is beyond its shelf life, it's out of date and we need a funding mechanism that works well for Wales. It is complicated, and I think that transparency is a question to be asked around the Barnett formula. And after all these years and other debates, it's reasonable to ask whether it remains the right mechanism for funding the different parts of the United Kingdom. But again, if we're going to reform it, we need to do so carefully and based on evidence, to have a system that's fair, transparent and properly reflects the needs of Wales, without putting our existing funding at risk.

I was grateful to the Cabinet Minister for pointing out the wording of the motion here today about the operation of the Barnett formula, because there is a very real risk that a full-scale review, without appropriate mitigations in place, could actually see us in a worse place. We need to have a grown-up discussion about that as well.

We know the Institute for Fiscal Studies estimated that, in 2024-25, Welsh Government received around 25 per cent more funding per person than was spent on comparable services in England. That's an important figure to keep in mind when we consider the Barnett formula—a formula that, of course, was agreed by the Conservative UK Government all those years ago, with that extra support in place recognising the needs of people here in Wales.

The third part of the motion, in relation to rail—the support for the £14 billion commitment to rail infrastructure in Wales is significant, but what matters, of course, to passengers is what actually gets delivered. We need to see projects that are going to be accelerated, sufficient funding being made available and communities across Wales actually benefiting from this investment across all of Wales. People will only feel the system's working when they can get to work well, when businesses can access markets and when our communities have the transport infrastructure they deserve.

We absolutely agree that the Welsh and UK Governments should be working together to deliver for the people of Wales. So, as Welsh Conservatives, Llywydd, we support this motion in front of us today. We support the greater fiscal flexibility. We support a review of the operation of the Barnett formula. We support the £14 billion commitment to rail, while making clear that we want to see investment delivered across all of Wales, alongside asking for greater flexibility and a fairer funding system, and also making sure that every £1 Wales already receives is spent wisely. Diolch yn fawr iawn.

Firstly, I'm amazed to hear that Reform don't think that fair funding is important and don't want more money for Wales. That's quite a statement. [Interruption.] Even though I wouldn't want to bore you, Cai, I'll crack on.

My comments are in relation to the Barnett formula. As we've heard, designed in the 1970s and, as we know, it was never designed to reflect need. Population is a key part of how it operates, but Wales isn't simply a smaller version of England. We've got an older population, higher levels of ill health, deprivation, greater rurality, and communities where delivering public services can cost significantly more. That's the fundamental problem for me. Barnett takes account of how many people live in Wales; it doesn't properly assess what Wales needs. Almost 50 years after it was introduced, I think we're entitled to ask whether that's still the right basis on which to fund our country. If we're serious about fairness, then need has to play a much greater role in how Wales is funded. Reform of Barnett is long, long overdue.

The reforms this Government are pursuing are important. We need to be able to see clearly how decisions are made, how spending is classified and how our share has been calculated, and we need independent oversight rather than leaving the Treasury effectively marking its own homework.

The funding rules also need to reflect the reality of devolution. If Wales takes responsibility for infrastructure, as we have with the core Valleys lines, then the way our funding is calculated should recognise that. I'm pleased that this Government is prepared to go further in the longer term and explore ultimately what could replace Barnett, because the Welsh fiscal framework already recognises something important: need matters. And these are precisely the kinds of things a fair funding system should take into account. Because surely the test shouldn't be whether every part of the UK gets the same amount per head, the test should be whether every part of the UK has the resources it needs to provide a comparable standard of public services. For me, that's where the debate now needs to go.

If the fundamental weakness of Barnett is that it doesn't properly assess need, then the starting point for whatever comes next should be a proper independent assessment of relative need across the nations of the UK, and it should be regularly updated so that our funding reflects the Wales we actually live in rather than relying on a formula that's inherited from the 1970s. That would be a much more rational basis for funding our public services.

And of course, as we've heard, Barnett is only one part of the wider fiscal settlement. The treatment of major infrastructure projects like HS2, control over the Crown Estate and the limits placed on Welsh Government borrowing all raise their own questions about whether Wales has a fair settlement and the freedom to invest in our own priorities. 

So, this motion isn't simply about making the existing system work a bit better, it's also about being prepared to ask what should come next, because almost 50 years after Barnett was introduced, we have the opportunity to do something we haven't really done before—to start with Wales, to start with the needs of our population and our communities, to look honestly at what it costs to deliver public services that people rely on and to make sure that we've got the resources and powers to invest properly in our future. That is, I think, a much stronger basis for a fiscal settlement than simply asking what Wales gets as a consequence of decisions made somewhere else. Ultimately, that's what fairness should mean—not asking Wales to fit the formula, but building a funding system that properly reflects us, a system where the rules are clear and independently overseen, where funding reflects the actual needs of our country and where we have greater control over the resources and fiscal levers we need to invest in our nation. Because after nearly 50 years of Barnett, we shouldn't be asking how much longer we can make an outdated funding formula work, we should be asking what a fair funding system for Wales looks like and be making the case for it. Diolch.

That is, I think, a much stronger basis for a fiscal settlement than simply asking what Wales gets as a consequence of decisions made somewhere else. Ultimately, that's what fairness should mean—not asking Wales to fit the formula, but building a funding system that properly reflects us, a system where the rules are clear and independently overseen, where funding reflects the actual needs of our country and where we have greater control over the resources and fiscal levers we need to invest in our nation. Because after nearly 50 years of Barnett, we shouldn't be asking how much longer we can make an outdated funding formula work, we should be asking what a fair funding system for Wales looks like and be making the case for it. Diolch.

Every local authority in Britain can move money into and out of reserves. This includes town and community councils and it actually includes school governing bodies, who can also move money into and out of reserves. No controls, no rules. It's their money, they can spend it or save it. Why is the Welsh Government treated differently? Once money is allocated to Wales or is raised in Wales, the Treasury has no legitimate interest in that money. This is the way they treat Westminster committees and how they treat different spending areas in Westminster. It is not the way to treat a Government.

Money is sometimes allocated late in the year, sometimes very late in the year. Money has been claimed back. There is an expectation it could have been carried forward, but that's only an expectation. The rules are really unfair. If not always able to carry it forward, money was claimed back. I did suggest at the time that we should not rely on the Treasury being fair—I don't think anybody's ever thought the Treasury was fair—and that we should actually take the money and spend it. We could give it to local authorities or give it to housing associations without any problem at all. But this is not a way to run a national budget. It does not cost the Treasury any money. Once it's here, it's here, and I don't see why they want to get involved in micromanaging Wales. It has to end. And once the money is allocated, then why does the Treasury want to get involved? It is not their money, they should be leaving us alone.

On funding, despite what has been said and believed, Wales does well out of the current system. We receive substantially more than we pay in. Estimates suggest that we collect about 70 per cent to 75 per cent of the per capita income in Wales. We spend about 110 per cent, including central Government expenditure, here in Wales. This is what being part of a larger country means—money is provided to those who need it most.

What should a funding system look like? Characteristics of a funding system for subnational Governments that were originally proposed by the Calman commission include: stability and predictability; simplicity and transparency; autonomy; efficiency; equity, so that resources are allocated in a way that takes account of relative need; and accountability, so that the link between decisions made and the tax paid by voters is clear. Any additional tax take within a region should impact on the budget available.

The Barnett formula evolved from the Goschen formula, which was designed specifically to preserve Scotland's public expenditure advantage over England. The formula was thus never designed with Wales in mind. Applied rigorously, the formula should have led to convergence in levels of spending per head across the UK. The formula has, however, preserved the spending advantage for Wales over England. There have been periodic adjustments to the operation of the formula since 1980, mainly through relative population changes. These adjustments have increased relative spending levels in Wales. The main advantage of the formula is its simplicity and objectivity as a basis for making spending allocations. There has been notable success in securing formula bypass since devolution. For example, Objective 1 match funding and funding for city deals. Northern Ireland has done substantially better in receiving money in excess of the Barnett formula. Remember, the Barnett formula calculates the minimum to be provided. Anything over and above that is allowed to be provided by the Government if they so desire.

We also have the Barnett floor. It was set following the Holtham commission investigation into the needs of Wales. At the 2015 spending review, the UK Conservative Government—see, Sam, I do mention the Conservatives—implemented a funding floor in Wales. This provided a guarantee that the Welsh Government block grant funding per head would not fall below 115 per cent of equivalent spending per head in England. Currently in Wales we get about 120 per cent of the equivalent funding per head in England. With the result of the Holtham review that Wales needs 115 per cent of the equivalent funding per head in England in devolved areas, if we get 120 per cent, we're doing well.

Currently, the total budget is £27.5 billion—£22.8 billion in revenue and £3.6 billion in capital. So, if Wales gets its 115 per cent, which is what Holtham said, then we get about £1 billion more than we should be getting, or than would be calculated. So, this idea that Wales is treated very badly by everybody might play well in certain circles, but it doesn't actually play with reality. This needs recalculating. I suggest academics, jointly appointed by the Welsh Government and the Treasury, at five-yearly intervals, should recalculate Wales's need. But remember, there's a danger that Wales will get less.

I support additional funding for rail. I have stations in my constituency that we need to be opening and reopening. Would money better be spent on transport in general? We need work doing on bus and rail interchanges. We need to ensure adequate parking near the new stations. What we do not need are rail lines to fulfil the wishes of the few passengers who want to use them.

contributions.text_english:
When the Prime Minister, Keir Starmer, made his way to Wales to announce £14 billion of investment to, as he put it, 'transform' Welsh rail, I'm sure many of us were hopeful that it was signalling the beginning of the end of historic underfunding for Welsh rail. However, as the details of commitments emerged, it became clear that, far from putting Wales on the right track, this commitment risks facilitating the continuation of underinvestment in Welsh rail over the current spending review period. It also, of course, made no effort to right the wrongs of the HS2 and the Oxford and Cambridge lines scandal. And whilst I'm sure we are glad to hear the new Prime Minister recently confirm that the £14 billion commitment remains firmly in place, I would maybe suggest to the Labour Party that it should have a word with Stephen Kinnock, the Secretary of State for Wales, given his views on this, as he doesn't quite seem to be on the same page as you in the Labour Party here, or even the Prime Minister.

Point 3 in today's motion does not set out to give Wales any special treatment or to secure any additional funding. Rather, the motion aims to ensure that the UK Government's commitment properly aligns with the delivery timelines of projects in Wales that have already been given the green light.

As the Cabinet Minister for Finance put it in her letter to the Chancellor:

'At this level of funding, the projects underpinning the commitment cannot be progressed at the pace required and key commitments will not be delivered within the planned timeframe.'

If we continue as we are, deadlines will be missed, projects will be in limbo, jobs could be at risk, and rail in Wales will continue to lag behind the rest of the UK. I therefore urge you all to support this motion today.

contributions.text_english:
Devolution should never mean a transfer of responsibility without the means to discharge it, and yet, too often in Wales, we've been given the powers we have so far without the funds to use them, trying to meet our responsibilities with one hand tied behind our backs, and that erodes public confidence in devolution.

I welcome this debate. It has shown me, actually, that there is a significant amount of cross-party support for the three points in the motion. Just to touch on them very quickly, the Wales reserve: if a Government does not need to spend money in one year, it should be able to save it for what is needed in the next year. That's exactly how we all do our own budgets at home. If we don't spend it, we can carry it over, and, therefore, that should be the same application to our budget here in Wales. Scotland does not face the same constraints. It has unlimited annual drawdowns from its own reserve.

The need for flexibility, though, goes beyond the reserve. Last July, Members across this Senedd agreed that it makes little sense for a national Government to have less borrowing flexibility than a local council, as has been raised by Mike Hedges. We remain stuck, with an overall capital borrowing cap whose real value is eroded by inflation over the past decade.

Secondly, the Crown Estate. Borrowing and revenue have to go hand in hand. Wales has a revenue stream in sight, and, at the moment, it is being collected elsewhere. The Crown Estate's Welsh assets were valued at £853 million in 2022-23, and 93 per cent of that is tied to offshore wind and marine energy. Of course, devolving that revenue would come with a reduction in the block grant—we do know that. But, just as in Scotland, the way that adjustment is calculated matters. If it is set transparently and reflects the growth of offshore wind in Wales, it could give us the much-needed means to invest in our own coastline and communities.

On the Barnett formula, I welcome the motion's language of review, fairness and transparency. But we must, as has been said, be cautious, as the Institute for Fiscal Studies has noted. Reopening the formula could cost Wales as readily as it benefits. So, the credible route is not a leap in the dark; it is, as has been said, a rigorous, evidence-based process. At present, the Treasury acts as judge, jury and executioner in disputes. We've seen that HS2 is the clearest example, and the Oxford to Cambridge line as well. When the same decision goes against Wales twice and no-one outside the Treasury can overturn it, that is not an error, it is a flaw in the design. What we need is an independent fiscal commission, along the lines of Australia's Commonwealth Grants Commission.

Finally, on rail, I welcome the commitment to £14 billion-worth of investment, and I support, of course, devolving rail infrastructure to Wales, as Scotland has. I have to refer us to the modicum of confusion that there was in the last Senedd over the £14 billion and the befuddlement and confusion in terms of the motions coming forward to us. But let's move on from that, as we should see, in terms of our railways. We need to see that rail devolution come to Wales, with the money attached to it, and we need to make sure that that affects the whole of Wales.

To finish, I ask the Welsh Government to be bolder in what it asks for, and I ask the UK Government, in turn, to give us a fair hearing into a fair settlement. Diolch yn fawr iawn.

contributions.text_english:
Diolch, Lywydd. To Reform, and to Cai Parry-Jones, may I start by saying that this Senedd most definitely should be discussing how we are funded? You tabled a debate last week on blankets of the past. I tabled one this week on the financing of Wales. Reform, you may be counting views and shares on social media. I'm counting the money made available and used in Wales. So, this motion is clear: it supports flexible access to reserves to enable better financial planning and control by Government, and that will definitely benefit the people of Wales.

Secondly, it supports better operation and transparency on the decisions that finance Wales via Barnett. These decisions should not be hidden behind a Treasury curtain. And it calls for rail investment in Wales to finally be realised, and those Burns stations, so often mentioned in this Senedd, to be built.

This motion today is not about the fiscal review; it's about the operation of Barnett. It is different to the call—.  It was seeking to create a consensus, a commonsense consensus, across this Chamber that you've decided that you don't sign up to.

It was good to hear the commonsense approach by the Conservatives, speaking of appropriate powers for appropriate use, and that's what good politics means. [Interruption.] Look at the detail of what's in front of you. Others have suggested and said quite clearly that we need to not lay on our laurels and remain just on what this motion today is seeking to create for the Senedd, but to be bolder—Jane Dodds's words; Carrie Harper also made that call.

I would say also, Mike Hedges, I will use that line when I next speak to the UK Treasury, when you reminded us all that school governing bodies and local authorities have more fiscal powers and borrowing powers than this Senedd itself has, on access to reserves in particular. You said the UK Treasury should not be micromanaging the finances of Wales, and that's a very important thing for us to get them to understand.

So, we've created a consensus here today. It doesn't include Reform. I won't lose any sleep over that. But if I can finish by just saying that these proposals in this motion are rooted in partnership, fairness and a shared cross-party ambition to improve outcomes for the people of Wales. And if that wasn't worth an hour of this Senedd's time, then I don't know what could be.

tabled_texts.text_english:
Motion NDM9307 Heledd Fychan, Lynne Neagle

To propose that the Senedd:

1. Calls on the Welsh and UK Governments to work together to:

a) enhance the Welsh Government’s fiscal flexibilities, including removal of all restrictions on the Wales Reserve;

b) review the operation of the Barnett Formula to strengthen fairness and transparency; and

c) reaffirm support for the commitment of £14 billion for rail infrastructure in Wales and accelerate delivery and sufficient funding for improvement projects across Wales during the current spending review period.
tabled_texts.text_original:
Cynnig NDM9307 Heledd Fychan, Lynne Neagle

Cynnig bod y Senedd:

1. Yn galw ar Lywodraeth Cymru a Llywodraeth y Deyrnas Unedig i gydweithio i:

a) gwella hyblygrwydd cyllidol Llywodraeth Cymru, gan gynnwys dileu'r holl gyfyngiadau ar Gronfa Wrth Gefn Cymru;

b) adolygu’r ffordd y mae Fformiwla Barnett yn gweithredu er mwyn cael mwy o degwch a thryloywder; ac

c) ailddatgan y gefnogaeth i'r ymrwymiad o £14 biliwn ar gyfer seilwaith rheilffyrdd yng Nghymru a chyflymu’r gwaith cyflawni a sicrhau cyllid digonol ar gyfer prosiectau gwella ledled Cymru yn ystod cyfnod yr adolygiad gwariant cyfredol.
Gohiriwyd y pleidleisio tan y cyfnod pleidleisio.
Daeth y cyfarfod i ben am 18:13.
